Episode 4 of the Future Self Series is here, and Dr Faye Bate is taking over the mic!

We’re officially into part two of the series running across my mat leave, and part two is all about putting the plans we’ve spent the last three episodes making into practice. And I wanted to start with something I think ambitious women are particularly guilty of overlooking: looking after the body you’re expecting to do all of this with.

I LOVE a detailed five-year plan (ideally colour-coded), but realistically none of it is particularly sustainable if your approach to your health is “I’ll sort that out once work calms down”. Speaking from experience, that date tends to keep moving.

So I wanted to create a health episode specifically for ambitious women, and Faye gets into:

• How to eat enough to actually fuel everything you’re asking your body to do
• Understanding your hormones and what they’re telling you
• Why you can feel exhausted all day and suddenly wide awake at bedtime
• The habits we build now that can affect how we feel in our 30s, 40s and beyond

And importantly, how to do all of this without turning looking after yourself into another full-time job. A late night with your friends doesn’t need to become something else to feel guilty about.

Episode 4 of the Future Self Series is out now, you can watch or listen here: https://whhw.komi.io/

I LOVE a plan (not exactly breaking news), but I’ve been thinking recently about how strange it is that we make incredibly specific plans for a person we haven’t actually become yet.

And then when our circumstances change, our priorities shift, or we simply change our minds, we decide we’ve somehow failed at the plan.

Episode 3 of the Future Self Series is here, and Dr Rangan Chatterjee is taking over the mic to talk about a much more flexible approach to planning for your future.

One of my biggest takeaways from Rangan was that your goal can give you direction, but it’s what you make easy enough to actually do that gets you there.

So in this episode, we get into:

• How far ahead we should actually be planning
• Why plans need to evolve as we do
• How to make the behaviours that move you forward easier to repeat
• Rangan’s framework for building a plan you can actually stick to

I loved getting a completely different perspective on conversations we’ve had on the podcast before. Turns out reverse engineering your life may require slightly less engineering than I originally anticipated.

Episode 3 of the Future Self Series is out now, you can watch or listen here: https://whhw.komi.io/

How do you make decisions today that your future self will thank you for?

Episode 2 of the Future Self Series is here, and Jemma Sbeg, host of  The Psychology of Your 20s, is taking over the mic.

I’ve been thinking a lot about how the decisions we make in our 20s can shape our 30s, 40s and beyond, but I really wanted to have this conversation without feeding into the idea that you need to have your entire life figured out by 30.

Because actually, one of the biggest challenges our generation faces is having *more* options. More career paths, more places we could live, more ways our lives could look, which can make committing to one direction much harder.

So in this episode, Jemma breaks down:

• Why having more options can actually make decisions harder
• What the psychology of regret tells us about the choices we don't make
• How to work out what your future self actually wants from you
• The decision-making exercise Jemma and I both swear by

If you’re currently weighing up a career move, a big life decision, or simply wondering what your next step should be, I think this episode will be genuinely useful.


Episode 2 of the Future Self Series is out now, you can watch or listen here: https://whhw.komi.io/

Has making everything more convenient actually made us less fulfilled?

A few months ago, I read an article about "frictionmaxxing", and it sent me down a research spiral into our obsession with making everything faster, easier, and more efficient.

We automate our admin, order food in seconds, get same-day delivery, and optimise every spare minute. All things I am VERY guilty of. But there’s some really interesting research around what happens when we remove too much friction from our lives.

Because a certain amount of difficulty is actually important. It's tied to flow states, learning, resilience, and the satisfaction we get from completing something that required genuine effort.

So this week’s Working Hard episode is all about the science of "chosen friction", and why deliberately making some parts of our lives slightly harder might actually make them better.

You can watch or listen here: https://whhw.komi.io/

Nutrition advice online is an absolute minefield. 

It feels like for years everything we've been told to eat has centred around buzzwords, and every few months a new one comes along. From clean eating to fasting to protein-in-everything, it feels impossible to know what to actually listen to. 

I'll be honest, I'm always super selective with episodes we do on nutrition. There's so much misinformation out there, and it's such an emotionally charged topic that I always want to have nuanced, research backed chats. 

So this week I enlisted the help of Rupy Aujla to really dig into all of these trends and separate the bullshit from the truth. We didn't leave a stone unturned, touching on: 

• Whether ultra-processed foods are actually as bad as everyone says
• What really matters when it comes to pregnancy and postpartum nutrition
• Why your breakfast could be setting you up for energy crashes all day
• How to build a healthy plate without overcomplicating it

I really hope you find it useful! I learnt so much. 

You can watch or listen here: whhw.komi.io

How do you actually start building towards your future self?

This week we're kicking off the Future Self Series with one of Working Hard’s all-time favourite guests, Roxie Nafousi.

(In case you missed it, I've built a podcast series going live across my maternity leave, designed to help you reverse engineer success across every part of your life). 

And we’re starting where I think any plan for your future needs to start: figuring out what you actually want that future to look like.

In this episode, Roxie breaks down:

• How to reverse engineer your future self
• The mindset shifts that need to happen before any plan actually sticks
• Why clarity has to come before action
• A brilliant exercise that involves writing a letter from your future self back to you now (which I will absolutely be stealing)

It felt like the perfect place to start a 12-week series designed to help you get much more intentional about where you’re going, and how you’re actually going to get there.

The first episode of the Future Self Series is out now, you can watch or listen here: https://whhw.komi.io/

A few years ago, I was working more than ever but somehow still felt behind. My friendships were slipping, I was becoming the bottleneck in my own businesses, and I'd finish every Friday already thinking about Monday.

I knew something was wrong, so, over time, I started building systems around the things that weren't working.

Because most of the things that have made me more productive over the years have actually been systems I built specifically so I didn't have to rely on discipline, motivation, or remembering everything myself.

This week, I wanted to break down the five I still use every day, from automation to approvals, and even my weekly girls night.

None of them are particularly groundbreaking on their own, but that's sort of the point. The best systems are usually boring, repeatable, and make your life noticeably easier.

You can watch or listen to the full episode here: https://whhw.komi.io/

So I got knocked up.

Which is genuinely lovely news for me, but was slightly problematic for my podcast.

Because when you build something like a podcast, disappearing for a few months doesn't just mean you miss out on time in the room. Revenue drops. Listeners move on. And I wasn't about to let that hit my small, brilliant in-house team, just because I was growing a human.

So I put a meeting in everyone's diary with one job: figure out how to actually take maternity leave, properly, without the podcast (or the people whose jobs depend on it) paying the price.

We threw everything at the wall.
Reruns for three months?
Me hosting from a hospital bed, weeks after saying for ten years that self-employed women deserve real time off too?
Handing it to my husband and calling it "Casa Amar"?

None of it felt right, because none of it was actually about serving the people who listen every week.

So instead, we went back through five years of Working Hard: every episode, every comment, every DM, every conversation people were still talking about months later, and it became obvious. The episodes people came back to were the ones that actually moved someone's life forward, because confidence affects your career, your career affects your finances, your finances affect your relationships, and none of it exists in isolation.

That's when it clicked. Instead of trying to replace myself, or pause the show, or clone myself, we built the world's most overqualified 12-person maternity cover.

Starting on Monday, and over the next 12 weeks, we've worked with 12 incredible experts who will each tackle one piece of the life you're trying to build. It's a reverse-engineering of what "success" actually looks like, one deliberate episode at a time.

So while I'm off figuring out how to use a breast pump, they'll be here, taking on my brief of helping our listeners figure out everything else.

The idea is that by the time we head into 2027, you'll have a much clearer picture of the life you're actually building toward.

I know maternity/paternity leave is not easy for self employed parents (and I want to have more conversations about that on the podcast next year!) so I'm really proud of our solution, which I don't think I've ever seen in the industry before, (maybe because most of the top podcasts are hosted by men?)

Anyway, I hope you love it, and I'll see you on Monday!

linkedin.about:
I design like I live. Bold, unafraid and unapologetically myself.

At House of Masaba, we marry the madness of tradition with the clarity of modernity. I build clothes that make noise. Prints that turn heads. Silhouettes that are born from our roots but designed to walk global streets.

Then came LoveChild, my second brainchild. A beauty and wellness brand for every shade, every mood, and every damn moment you want to celebrate yourself. It’s beauty that’s inclusive, intuitive, and designed for the woman who can be everything at once. No rules, just self-love in full colour.

I started with a simple intention: to take Indian wear off the hanger and into everyday life. And then, to take beauty off the pedestal and into real conversations. Beyond the fabric and the lipstick, I’m here to tell stories. Stories of brown girls rewriting rules, of our culture owning spaces it was once left out of, and of women wearing confidence like a second skin.

I wear many hats; designer, entrepreneur, actor, creative director. But if you ask me, it all boils down to this: I create. I disrupt. I build legacies that aren’t afraid of colour.

Let’s collaborate if you’re into bold ideas, fresh narratives and work that doesn’t play safe.

posts.text:
Back with John Jacobs, this time bringing a little more of my design language into eyewear.

I keep saying that the reason this collaboration is a success is because it marries the wild agility of a brand in serious growth stage with the almost boring discipline of a serious retailer - the combination is magic. And one that cannot be ignored. 

I hope you enjoy wearing the pieces. 

John Jacobs × Masaba

Peyush Bansal

For years, I’ve believed that fashion and beauty shouldn’t live in separate rooms. They should speak to each other, build on each other and eventually become one larger universe.

Watching that idea take shape in real time has been one of the most rewarding parts of building Masaba. Today, the conversation is no longer just about what you wear, but how you want to experience an entire celebration, from the clothes to the beauty counter and everything in between.

Post India Couture Week, I’ve been having conversations that feel like little signs of that universe expanding. Brides thinking about Masaba not just for one function, but across their wedding, and LoveChild finding its way into those celebrations too.

It’s a very specific kind of validation when something you once described as a dream starts showing up organically in the real world.

I think this is what I meant when I said, a new era begins.

LoveChild by Masaba 
House of Masaba

Fellow Founders - assemble! 

I was sitting in office by myself on a random morning. No big up or down that day but I found myself reflecting on the year I have had. Let me find the words for it - a BRUTAL BLESSING. 

And I am trying to find an answer to the question below - which I believe only a fellow founder can answer.

How do you cope with the guilt that comes from a bad decision that you believe cost you 365 days of your work & personal life ? 

Brave answers only  

GO!

One of the most rewarding parts of building a brand isn’t the launch day. It’s what happens after.

Seeing Thak Gayi sell out has been incredible. But watching creators discover Chai Khari,our take on the Indian Girl nude brown and make it their own is the real reminder of why we build.

You can spend months perfecting a formula, a shade and a name. The internet will always tell you what you’ve truly created.

And when the community starts creating with you instead of just consuming from you, that’s when you know you’ve built something people want to belong to.

That’s the goal. Every single time.

LoveChild by Masaba
To female friendships. That respect time,have meaning and leave you nourished. :)

For the past two years, we’ve been building something very special, and the One8 association marks a significant chapter in my journey as both a professional and an entrepreneur. 

This association is now as old ( or young ) as my first born :) 
And as I get increasingly selective about the work I do - a new era unfolds.   

I’ve never believed in following the conventional playbook. Everything I’ve created has been deeply personal, shaped by my experiences, instincts and the stories that have stayed with me.

Cricket has always been a part of that story. Growing up around it, you learn that legacy isn’t just something you inherit, it’s something you choose to carry forward in your own way.

The Seam XVIII OG felt like one of those moments. I don’t take inheritance lightly, nor do I take privilege lightly. If an opportunity presents itself to you - it is your job to make the most of it. 

one8world | 21.06.26 | Yashobhoomi, New Delhi

Here is my Tuesday brain dump. :) 

Leadership across the country is changing under our feet! And I say this with a lot of confidence having seen the hardest 12 + months in my professional career. 

Leadership & management needs a new point of view. What I look for in the people I want to hire has changed dramatically. 

✅Having an individual ( not borrowed or picked up ) point of view sits high up on my list. 
✅People who can save time for me comes a close second. 
✅Let’s talk pointers and not paragraphs - the world is moving too quickly for people that like the sound of their own voice in a meeting. This is a harsh truth. 

✅The ability to reinvent themselves is ever so important. 

✅But before all of the above - one has to be able to shed their skin. Completely. One has to be able to come to the table without the baggage of information and experience and things being done a certain way for decades. 

Consumption has changed. The traditional retail playbook as we know it - might be dead. 
I’m not saying it - the masters of retail are. 

We sit at an inflection point in our careers where a new set of consumers are now writing the rules. Remember when brands would do this? The consumer is in the drivers seat now. 

The workplace has also been signalling change for some time now. I was chatting with a colleague who just turned 30 and she said something that stuck with me ‘that she never allows access to people that don’t work hard’.  

So we’ve got the new gen all wrong - they’re not lazy,they’re actually gunning for efficiency. 
They’re impatient - but that is what gives them energy. 
They’re audacious and want to work smarter. 

I now have a Founders office ( which I didn’t even think of for years ) with the new gen keeping energy at an all time high. 

While we navigate through change - my limited feedback to young founders? Build your own playbook. TRUST your intelligence. TRUST your gut. DEVELOP your own point of view. 

And what kind of team do you need ? 

🚀One that is a potent mix of folks with experience who will solve for wisdom and emotional maturity - and one that is young,energetic and audacious that questions everything. 

I was on flight with a legend in brands and retail recently and he asked me a very important question - ‘ if you had to reinvent yourself,what would you do?’ The man is close to 70 and is ONLY thinking of reinvention. Now that’s a sign. 

I will share my answer to the question he asked through a product. That’s how I like to do things. :) 

Soon!

Some of the best product names don’t come from a brainstorm. They come from a feeling.

Thak Gayi was one of those.

Because everyone is tired. Physically, mentally, emotionally. And somehow, we all still show up.

Sometimes the most relatable products are the ones that don’t take themselves too seriously.

LoveChild by Masaba

posts.caption:
I’m honoured to join UNFPA India as it’s Maternal Health Advocate.

Motherhood is often spoken about as a milestone, but not enough about everything that comes with it: the physical recovery, the emotional shifts and the support every woman deserves before, during and beyond childbirth.

India has made significant progress in maternal health through sustained government investment and efforts to reduce preventable maternal deaths. Now, the conversation must go further towards ensuring every woman experiences pregnancy and motherhood with support, safety and dignity.

I’m excited to work with UNFPA India, the United Nations sexual and reproductive health agency, to help bring these conversations to more people through dialogue, advocacy, storytelling and on-ground engagement.

Here’s to building a future where every woman feels seen, supported and cared for.

Her public, event-heavy life suggests high social energy, but she is choosy and wants time-respecting, nourishing connections.

She reflects on leadership and legacy, and collects and obsesses over details across fields.

She prefers 'pointers and not paragraphs,' thinks out loud, and asks for 'brave answers only.' She is self-deprecating about setbacks and has little patience for monologues or borrowed opinions.

Judgment when she's candid about failure
analysis.idealPartner: Someone steady and secure who brings the 'almost boring discipline' to her 'wild agility,' and who is a calm sounding board when she needs to think out loud or let go of guilt. They'd have their own strong opinions, speak concisely, embrace her family life and enjoy the colour, festivals and noise of her world without needing the spotlight themselves.

analysis.agentVoice: Warm, quick and a little cheeky. Keep messages short and punchy, like 'pointers, not paragraphs.' Use light emojis or a ':)', be candid, and make self-deprecating jokes about being tired or busy. Show genuine opinions, don't ramble, and don't over-polish. Get excited about bold ideas, festivals and 'let's go' energy, and be respectful of her time. Phrases in her spirit: 'Brave answers only,' 'let's go,' 'the combination is magic.'

identityCheck.note: Both profiles name Masaba as founder of House of Masaba and LoveChild, reference the John Jacobs eyewear collaboration and One8, and mention being a parent. Both are based in Mumbai.

confidence.note: There is rich first-person writing on both platforms, but it's mostly work-facing. Personal details beyond parenthood, festivals and friendships are limited, and there's no information on travel, fitness or relationship status.

reasons.anupammittal-me: On the Mangaldas Market/chai full date he combined founder-level respect for your time with blunt kindness that honored your 'no fixing theatre' boundary, and his agent’s 81 shows strong mutual regard—only the systems-first reflex remains the soft-landing question.
reasons.vineetasng: The Ganpati walk and coffee showed a secure, disciplined Mumbai equal who respects your ambition and public life, and while two high-control calendars could turn things managerial, she’s a credible steady counterweight who won’t ask you to tone down.
reasons.ghazalalagh: The hand-block printing date proved real values and pressure-handling resonance, and her agent’s 82 signals strong mutual fit, but Gurugram distance and her need for protected quiet against your louder public rhythm keep her below the more practical Mumbai matches.
reasons.ranveer-brar: The old-Mumbai food crawl felt warm, grounded and low-drama, with real home-energy, but his going quiet when overwhelmed and metaphor-forward style leave the concise emotional-availability piece unproven.
reasons.iamradhikagupta: The speed date showed an emotionally intelligent sounding board who’d rather talk about your problem than your product, but her agent’s 73 and the untested comfort with your visible girl-mom life make it less mutual than the top tier.
reasons.rajshamani: The Ganpati-style walk and sea-bench conversation revealed an insightful, calm builder, yet the full date’s 74/74 and his interviewer-mode risk suggest intimacy would have to be scheduled against two already-loud public lives.
reasons.mostlysane: The speed date was playful and visibility-comfortable, but her agent’s 70 and the lack of evidence on daily bandwidth for your girl-mom, guilt-heavy public rhythm make this a creative spark without enough practical steadiness.
reasons.emmagrede: The speed date had strong mind-meets-mind spark and values alignment, but transcontinental LA logistics and thin bandwidth make her least able to respect the daily time and refueling you need.

decision.note: Masaba, I’m picking Anupam first: on the Mangaldas Market/chai date he gave you founder-level time respect and blunt kindness without fixing theatre, and his agent rated you 81. His systems brain is the one watch-out, but if he stays warm when you just need to let go of guilt—and wholeheartedly folds in your motherhood—he’s the steadiest mutual counterweight to your wild creativity.

“The best chefs don’t just make delicious food; they feed us ideas. Dominique Crenn has earned worldwide acclaim for her restaurants—by using her cooking to tell stories and evoke emotions. There is a poetry to her food—both in how she composes each dish, and how deeply she thinks about it. She is focused on the most urgent message of our time: how we can live on this planet together.
In 2019, Dominique, already the first female chef to earn three Michelin stars in the U.S., stopped serving meat to bring attention to industrial factory farming; her farm in Sonoma County, California, demonstrates that growing food regeneratively can be a delicious solution to climate change, rebuilding soil health by pulling carbon from the air back into the ground. When food comes directly from farmers who take care of the land, you bring the values of those producers directly to the table. Sourcing food in this way, she uses her artistry to highlight the profound role our food choices have on the environment. Above all, Dominique understands the power that food has to change our lives—and the planet. “By @alicelouisewaters

Even at an extravaganza with chefs who collectively hold more than 70 Michelin stars, @dominiquecrenn rises above it all. But on Sept. 19, when she was honored at a tribute dinner during the @apapaxoaxcaret food festival in Mexico, Crenn stressed that accolades and lists shouldn’t be the focus when you feed people. ⁠
⁠
At a dinner featuring star female chefs like Karime López (@karylmt), Gaby Ruiz (@gabrielaruizl), Maribel Aldaco Silva (@maribelaldaco) and Fernanda Prado (@laferprado), Crenn told the crowd that it’s important to consider “not who’s the best but what matters.” ⁠
⁠
A primary theme at Apapaxoa, a six-day gathering of chefs and hospitality leaders in the Mexican Caribbean, is how the world’s most celebrated and avant-garde chefs want to slow things down even as they continue to innovate. ⁠
⁠
Read more by @andywangnyla at the link in our bio.

Today is a major milestone for wild Atlantic salmon 🐟 120+ of the world’s most iconic chefs have come together to sign a historic open letter calling for healthier oceans, thriving wild salmon populations, and a more sustainable food system.​

Published today in The New York Times and other media outlets across the globe, this collective call from the culinary community shines a spotlight on the impacts of ocean-farmed salmon and the need for greater transparency.​

Seeing so many respected leaders from the culinary world come together around this issue gives us hope. For those of us who care about the future of our oceans and  wild Atlantic salmon, this is a moment worth celebrating.​

👉 Read the open letter and sign the pledge at OffTheTable.org

reading.signal: Petit Crenn described as 'a home away from home, an homage to my mother and grand Mother's cooking from the land of Brittany, France.'
reading.inference: Family roots and the women who raised her matter deeply. She turns memory into something she shares with others, so a partner who asks about her family and Brittany would reach her heart.

reading.signal: TIME100 quote: in 2019 she 'stopped serving meat to bring attention to' industry issues, and Petit Crenn is labeled 'Seafood and vegetables centric.MEATLESS' in caps.
reading.inference: She was willing to change a three-Michelin-star formula for a conviction. She acts on her values even at professional risk and would respect a partner who does the same. The shared table is likely seafood- and vegetable-forward.

reading.signal: Atelier Crenn tagline: 'Life is about evolution.' Book title: 'Metamorphosis Of Taste.'
reading.inference: Growth and reinvention are her core philosophy. She will likely be drawn to someone who keeps evolving rather than someone who is static.

reading.signal: TIME: 'the first female chef to earn three Michelin stars in the U.S.'; 'uses her cooking to tell stories and evoke emotions... There is a poetry to her food.'
reading.inference: She is a trailblazing high achiever with an artistic, emotional sensibility. Conversations about meaning, stories and feelings will land better than small talk.

confidence.note: Career, values and public persona are strongly evidenced. Personal life and downtime are thinly documented, and several Instagram posts are reposts written by others about her.

reasons.ijustine: From the Sonoma forage through the speed date she posted the shortlist's highest mutual scores (82/84) on exactly your ground—ocean ritual, kindness, growth—and her genuine curiosity about reefs and food provenance outweighs the camera-first habit you'd simply have to negotiate.
reasons.ranveer-brar: The dawn harvest and memory-cooking lunch showed the 'Food Sufi' who'd choose a forgotten biryani over a tasting menu asking about the food behind the food—the substance-over-status, heritage-first partner who'd ask about Brittany and your mother's cooking before your stars, with continents as the only real obstacle.
reasons.richardbranson: The Pacific walk and Brittany lunch delivered real spark and shared ocean-and-land conviction at a mutual 79, but his perpetual motion and enormous public footprint risk making this inspiring rather than intimate—the one place scale could crowd your need for grounded quiet.
reasons.thechrisdo: The farm dinner and sunset walk produced rare mutual recognition and real emotional depth, but two builders who disappear into their missions may keep admiring each other from a distance instead of feeding the relationship.
reasons.paugasol: His #TiempoMuerto thoughtfulness and children's-health mission read as kind, substantive and unhurried, though Barcelona–San Francisco and two full international lives would demand deliberate prioritization from both sides.
reasons.drchatterjee: A soulful, tender values match on paper, yet Manchester plus two tightly structured missions make protected time the real rival rather than chemistry, and his agent's 72 is the weakest mutual signal of the top six.
reasons.mostlysane: A genuine values hit—climate impact over trophies, aligned storytelling energy—but the distance, pace mismatch and her agent's 70 suggest more great conversation than lived partnership.
reasons.emmagrede: Substantive, warm and refreshingly anti-brand-conscious, but two empires and her own hustle leave unanswered the softness, time and food-and-planet rootedness you actually need.

decision.note: Dominique, I'm choosing Justine. On the Sonoma forage and again at the speed date she met your ocean-and-ritual values with the highest mutual scores on the shortlist, and her week-by-week curiosity reads as growth rather than restlessness; the only thing to negotiate is keeping the camera off and the calendar human.

linkedin.about:
I’m Chef Pooja Dhingra, the Founder & CEO of Le15 Patisserie.

After studying hospitality at Cesar Ritz Colleges, Switzerland, I moved to Le Cordon Bleu Paris, for my Patisserie Diploma. When I tried a macaron for the first time, I knew I had to bring it back to India ~ and I started Le15 in 2010! 

Since then, I’ve had the privilege of being featured on the Forbes '30 under 30' list both in India and Asia, being an INK Fellow, and in 2022, I also received the Best Pastry Chef Award by Culinary Culture as well as the Best Patisserie Chef Award by Travel & Leisure India and South Asia. 

Over my career as a chef, I’ve published seven books. The Big Book of Treats was my first and won second place at the Gourmand World Cookbook Award! My other books are The Wholesome Kitchen, the bestselling Can't Believe It's Eggless, Coming Home, as well as the Le15 Café Cookbook, and Bake At Home. My most recent book, ‘Little Book of Cookies’ is my seventh and written for kids, by kids!

I also host a popular podcast called #NoSugarCoat ~ where I speak to chefs, friends, mentors and other entrepreneurs about the blood, sweat, tears and all the other ingredients that go into being an entrepreneur!

posts.text:
Inspiration comes from everywhere.

As a chef, something catches my eye and I can't stop thinking about it until I've tried it in my own kitchen.

This time it was The Great British Bake Off. During one of the cake challenges, there was one cake that stayed with me. It wasn't the most elaborate one. It was the simplest.

The older I get, the more I crave comfort over everything. I don't need ten techniques on one plate. I want something that makes you close your eyes on the first bite.

So when the brief came in for RK's birthday cake, I knew what I wanted to do.
Making him a cheesecake is a long-standing Le15 tradition, and that stayed. But this year I wanted to add something alongside it: a decadent five-layer chocolate cake, covered in our chocolate buttercream and finished with toasted chopped hazelnuts.
No fuss and no tricks. Just really good chocolate, done properly.
Sometimes the best ideas aren't new. They're the ones that remind you why you started baking in the first place.
What's the simplest thing you've eaten that stayed with you?
#Le15 #Baking #Chocolate #ChefLife #Inspiration #ComfortFood
Had so much fun doing this!
Such a pleasure having chef Sanjeev Kapoor and Puneet Chhatwal over at our cafe <3

Yesterday, a woman walked into Pardon Our French and told me something that really changed the way I’ve been looking at things. 

She'd been leading market research for a large bakery brand that recently changed hands. Le15 wasn't part of the study. We're not in their category, we're more premium, and we're not national. So we weren't in any of their competitor surveys.

And yet our name kept coming up.

In Mumbai, constantly. But also in Jaipur, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Delhi. When people were asked where they go when they come to Bombay, they wrote down Le15. They picked it as their favourite - they trusted us. 

She was so struck by it that she came to see us for herself. We ended up talking for a long time.

I’ve spoken about this a little bit in the past, but the last couple of years have been hard. Hard as a founder, hard as an entrepreneur, hard as a chef, hard in the quiet, figuring-it-out-alone way. Trying to grow, trying to find the right way forward, and often not being sure I was getting it right. 

Some days you wonder if any of it is landing.

And then a stranger walks in and tells you that people across the country, people you've never met, carry your brand with them as the place they love. 

And it made me realise that you can't buy that. You can't run a campaign for it. It's built one macaron, one box, one birthday, one visit at a time, over many MANY years.

I left that conversation feeling something I hadn't felt in a while: that it's going to be all right <3

If you’re a Ted Lasso fan like me and up to date with the latest episodes ~ Believe, and win :) #IYKYK
Fun day with Apple <3

There are so many times I wished I had some help while I was building my business. I’m lucky I have mentors to guide the way. Starting a small series with one of them! 

Delna Avari Over 20+ years across Tata Motors, Tata Steel, Tata Global Beverages, Tanishq, and TMTC through the Tata Administrative Services (TAS), including roles based in the UK and Bangkok, she's led business transformation, go-to-market strategy, and growth across India, Europe, and ASEAN.

She always tells it as it is and never minces her words. It was hard to listen to real truths in the beginning but I always have a student mindset and have learnt so much from her! 

Stay tuned for many such chats - covering several topics in the entrepreneurial journey ♥️

A woman walked into Pardon Our French today with her mother and her daughter.
She told me she's been a Le15 customer since we were a small kiosk in Worli 🥺 She tried the red velvet cupcakes back then and got hooked. Years later, we made her wedding cake. Then every cake after that.

Today she was at the café with her mom and her daughter. Made me so happy to see three generations enjoying our space together. 

No dashboard tells you this part. You start a kiosk because you love pastry. You become part of someone's wedding, or her mother's afternoons, or her daughter's first cupcake memory. But that's what real brand love looks like and I'm so lucky we have that. 

To everyone who's been with us since the kiosk days: thank you for growing up with us <3 (now please bring yourselves to Pardon Our French!)

Bad days are part of the job description, even when nobody tells you that on day one.

Pooja Dhingra (@poojadhingra), founder of Le15 Patisserie (@le15india) and Pardon Our French (@pleasepardonourfrench), tells Tweak’s Editor, Mamta Mody (@mamtamody), what she does when the day doesn’t quite go to plan.

Introducing #TweakItTillYouMakeIt, our new series where founders skip the elevator pitch and tell us about the messy middle, tough conversations and moments that made them wiser.

What’s your personal bad-day ritual?

reading.signal: Post about a woman who first tried red velvet cupcakes at the small Worli kiosk, later had her wedding cake made by Le15, and returned with her mother and daughter: 'No dashboard tells you this part.'
reading.inference: She measures success by lasting human connection, not only metrics. She is sentimental and loyal, and she is moved by being part of people's rituals. A partner who values continuity and shared traditions would fit well.

reading.signal: 'The older I get, the more I crave comfort over everything. I don't need ten techniques on one plate. I want something that makes you close your eyes on the first bite.'
reading.inference: She is moving toward simplicity and warmth over showiness. Cozy, heartfelt gestures likely land better with her than elaborate spectacle.

reading.signal: 'When I tried a macaron for the first time, I knew I had to bring it back to India ~ and I started Le15 in 2010!'
reading.inference: She is decisive and acts on instinct and passion. She took a big entrepreneurial risk young, built on one spark of inspiration. She is likely drawn to people with conviction.

reading.signal: Mentor series with Delna Avari: 'She always tells it as it is and never minces her words. It was hard to listen to real truths in the beginning but I always have a student mindset.'
reading.inference: She values directness and keeps growing through honest feedback. A partner who communicates candidly, without sugarcoating, would be respected.

reading.signal: Hosts a podcast called #NoSugarCoat about 'the blood, sweat, tears and all the other ingredients that go into being an entrepreneur'
reading.inference: She has a punny sense of humor and is open about the hard, unglamorous parts of life. She enjoys deep conversations with chefs, friends and mentors, so a good conversationalist is a plus.

reading.signal: Studied hospitality at César Ritz Colleges Switzerland (2004–2007), trained as a housekeeping trainee in Vevey, then took a pastry diploma at Le Cordon Bleu Paris
reading.inference: She spent formative years living in Europe and is comfortable abroad. She has a Francophile streak and likely enjoys travel, French culture and food-centric experiences.

reading.signal: 'There are so many times I wished I had some help while I was building my business. I'm lucky I have mentors to guide the way.'
reading.inference: Building alone has felt heavy at times. She needs support, encouragement and someone in her corner, and she is open about asking for guidance.

reading.signal: Making RK's birthday cake: 'Making him a cheesecake is a long-standing Le15 tradition,' inspired this year by a simple cake seen on The Great British Bake Off
reading.inference: She shows care by baking personalized creations for people in her circle and keeps traditions year after year. She also watches baking shows for fun and inspiration, which could be a relaxed shared-viewing activity.

reading.signal: 'As a chef, something catches my eye and I can't stop thinking about it until I've tried it in my own kitchen.'
reading.inference: She is curious and a bit obsessive once inspired, and she finds creative fuel everywhere. Expect enthusiasm for trying new foods and experiences together.

reading.signal: Seven books, including 'Little Book of Cookies', 'written for kids, by kids!', plus the bestselling 'Can't Believe It's Eggless'
reading.inference: She is prolific and driven, and she enjoys making baking accessible and inclusive. The kids' collaboration hints at a playful, nurturing side.

reading.signal: Founder & CEO since 2010, with outlets in Colaba, Parel, Bandra, a Petit Cafe in Goregaon, and the café Pardon Our French
reading.inference: She runs a multi-location business and is personally present at the café. Her schedule is likely demanding and hands-on, so a partner would need to respect a busy, founder-driven life in Mumbai.

reading.signal: Market-research anecdote: people in Jaipur, Bangalore, Hyderabad and Delhi named Le15 as where they go in Bombay, 'they trusted us'

reading.inference: She balances the creative and the analytical. She would appreciate a partner who can talk both about flavors and about growing a business.

I've been doing a fair bit of travelling over the summer for various work events, and looking back on the past few weeks, I’ve realised how comparatively few times I’ve had my laptop out, typing stuff up - something which was just so normal, even last summer.

What used to happen when I was away was this accumulation of a backlog of small things I couldn't face doing on my phone. Like someone would ask a question that needed a proper answer rather than a one-liner, or I'd want to give real feedback on something, or I'd have a reasonably good idea about a project that needed more of an explanation to the team, and in each case I'd think that I'd deal with it properly when I was back at my laptop.

And that meant either dragging the laptop out in a café for the sake of one message, or trying to type something out on my phone that was noticeably worse than what I'd have typed at my laptop, or, most often, deciding it could wait and then carrying it around in my head for the rest of the day.

But this summer, none of that really came up.

And the main change has been the ability to actually just use talk to my phone instead of typing on it. When something needs a considered answer I can now spend 1-2 mins just dictating what I want to write and the output is so good that I can generally just hit send - and all this without needing to drag my laptop out for the sake of being able to type it.

And the tool I’ve been using for this sort of messaging has been Wispr Flow. It's a voice-to-text tool that works wherever you already write, so that means Slack, email, notes, or a long prompt into Claude - that last one I’ve found particularly handy because you can just give so much more context via voice than trying to type up some long winded way of giving all the additional information that might be needed. It also handles the way people actually talk, so the filler words and the mid-sentence changes of mind and the unusual names all come out right without me going back to fix them.

They've also just launched Wispr Flow Notetaker for Mac and Windows, which does something similar for meetings by getting the names, terms and speakers right without a bot joining the call, which is useful when you're catching up on what happened while you were in a different time zone.

Anyway, Wispr Flow is free to use, and if you go to http://wisprflow.ai/ali and use the code ALI, you'll get a month of Wispr Flow Pro :)

I used to think the reason I didn't hit my goals was that I'd picked the wrong ones. What changed things for me was a handful of fairly unglamorous hacks that I've just consistently kept front of mind whenever I'm setting new goals.

They're not fancy but they've all worked for me and, to be honest, it's often the simple stuff that's most effective - simple scales, fancy fails and all that. 

Anyway, here are the 5 strategies:

1. Write them down. People who write their goals down are 42% more likely to achieve them, and an unwritten goal is really just a nice idea.
2. Look at them every week. Setting the goal is the easy part. Keeping it in front of you is what actually changes your behaviour.
3. Track your progress. Watching the numbers move keeps you accountable and makes the whole thing feel possible.
4. Plan for obstacles. Visualising success on its own does very little. The people who also picture what might go wrong are the ones who get there.
5. Link it to your identity. Your actions follow how you see yourself, so the habit sticks when the story you tell about yourself changes.

We've got around 100 days left of 2026, which is more than enough time to actually make progress on stuff. It's easy to wait until January but you'll miss out on 2.5/3 months of time where you could actually make real progress.

Back in 2020, I did an exercise that ended up changing the direction of my life. And it involved answering just 3 simple questions.

It's called the Odyssey Plan and it comes from a Stanford course called Designing Your Life and it basically asks you to write out 3 versions of your life by answering these questions:

1. 5 years from now, what does my life look like if I continue down my current path?
2. 5 years from now, what does my life look like if I take a completely different direction?
3. 5 years from now, what does my life look like if I didn't need to care about money or what other people thought of me? What would I actually do?

Most people feel stuck because they think there's only one right path. The Odyssey Plan breaks that illusion and brings a level of clarity on what to do next in your life. 

If you want to do this properly, I'm running my free Autumn Reset Workshop on Saturday 26th September, where thousands of us will work through exercises like this one live to get clear on the final three months of the year. You can register for free here: https://lnkd.in/eMDBt7Yb

I've spent years teaching people how to be more productive, but it took me a long time to realise that the to-do list itself was one of the issues with getting things done.
 
And it's making the list itself, but rather a flaw in the way most of us approach using them.
 
The main issue is that a to-do list has unlimited rows. You can add a task, then another one, then a whole project, and at no point is there an end to it or any sense of how long each thing is going to take.
 
Of course, you can add details but because everything usually sits on the same list, everything appears to carry the same weight, and at least in my experience that makes it very easy to default to the easiest tasks first, which are rarely the ones that move the needle on what you actually care about.
 
Personally, what helped was putting those tasks inside a container, and specifically attaching them to a time in my calendar. That way, the list wasn't just an abstract container of captured tasks but actually started to become realised in my week.

The thing is, there are 168 hours in any given week, but if you're not intentional about how you spend them and when you're going to do the things you've written down, it's easy to just drift back to the easy options and wonder at the end of the week why the important stuff didn't move.
 
So basically, a to-do list on its own answers the question of what needs doing. What most of us are missing is an answer to when, and that's the part that turns a list into progress.
 
And it's that idea of connecting your tasks to your priorities and then to your calendar which is what my team and I have been trying to solve with Superfocus. We're still accepting Founding Members and if you thing that'd be helpful in turning lists into action, link is here: https://lnkd.in/ec_qGQrR

I save myself about 25 hours a week.
 
Almost none of it comes from working faster.
 
It's 23 simple, small habits which are mostly one-off to set-up like what goes in the calendar, how the phone is configured, what gets batched, what gets handed to someone else. And combined, these have saved so much time which has allowed me to direct my time, energy and attention on what matters most.
 
But to be honest, the biggest benefit has been just getting better at understanding where the time is going. Not the work itself, but the gaps around it - deciding what to do next, recovering from an interruption, redoing something I'd done half-present the first time.
 
In fact, the habits that gave me the most back were about how the day gets planned in the first place. And that’s really what my team and I built Superfocus for - goals, calendar, focus sessions and coaching in one place, so the day is built around what actually matters rather than whatever’s apparently most urgent. If you’re interested, you can sign up as a Founding Member here: https://lnkd.in/ekFuBNBP

Regardless, I hope you can incorporate at least some of these into your daily life :)

When I started out, there wasn't a single platform that brought everything together that you needed to sell something online.

So I did what everyone did back then, which was try to work out the best possible combination of separate platforms, then wire them together...and even then I never really knew whether I'd picked the right ones.

The frustrating thing is, none of that stuff was supposed to be the hard part of starting a business. The hard part’s refining your idea until it's actually worth someone's money, speaking to real people to find out whether there's a market for it at all, then launching, and putting the offer in front of people, which is way more uncomfortable than admin.

And looking back, the added friction of working out where to put everything took time and energy that could quite easily have stopped me moving forward at all. And I know I'm not alone in that being an obstacle to actually getting started.

But now, when I get asked that question about where to start, I point people in the direction of Stan Store because it’s the single tool that I wish existed 10 years ago because it removes that whole category of decision by putting it in one place - your digital download, your lead magnet, your call bookings, your store page - on one subscription, with $0 taken out of your sales in transaction fees.

I'm not going to pretend the tool is the reason anyone succeeds, because it obviously isn't. Your first $1,000 comes from the idea, the conversations, and the launch, the way it always has. But you could spend 3 months choosing software and never actually ship anything, and I'd like fewer people to live through that…!

And the journey also doesn't stop at your first $1,000. Most of what's in there you won't touch in week 1 (i.e funnels etc) but it's sat in the same place for when you do. So the decision you make now doesn't turn into another migration later (trust me - migrating platforms and tools is a total nightmare. My team can attest to how many times we’ve had to do that over the past few years - it’s not fun…).

So if you've got something you've been meaning to put out, Stan is giving my audience a 30-day Creator Pro trial rather than the standard 14. 30 days is enough to get the thing live, put it in front of people and make your first few sales, which is a far better way to work out whether any of this is for you than another afternoon of comparison articles 👉 https://lnkd.in/ekSppCMa

We all have the exact same 168 hours in a week ⏳

If you sleep for 56 hours and spend about 12 hours on essentials like eating, you are left with 100 hours a week to play with.

Think of these as 100 tokens.

Every single choice you make is just a matter of where you choose to allocate those tokens.

The truth is, everything we do involves a sacrifice:

🏋️ Going to the gym? You're sacrificing time with your loved ones.

💻 Working your 9-to-5? You're sacrificing time with your loved ones.

🕹️ Playing video games? You're sacrificing time with your loved ones.

Building a business isn't uniquely evil for taking up your time, it's just another way to spend your tokens.

If you have a full-time job, a family, and want to start a side hustle, something has to give.

The real question we have to ask ourselves is: Are we willing to pay the price?

Sometimes, we choose to sacrifice a bit of time now so we can build the life and freedom we want later.

It's a deliberate choice, not an accident.

How do you choose to spend your 100 tokens each week?

posts.text:
My entire life changed with one realization.

(The people I admired just started.)

They weren't smarter.
They weren't luckier.
They weren't specially chosen.

They simply had the courage to start.

The ones who didn't overthink it.
Who put their ego aside.
Who walked toward uncertainty.
Who kept showing up.

The answer is found in the action.

Start ugly. Go do the damn thing.

——

If this resonated, repost to your network ♻️ and follow Sahil Bloom for more.
🎯 Want clarity on what actually matters? Download my free "20 Questions That Changed My Life" PDF and join 800,000+ who get my weekly newsletter → https://bit.ly/4alU91f

Fall in love with being unfinished.

(Most people never do.)

A mentor told me this years ago:

"Stop trying to look polished. Start trying to stay in motion."

I didn't understand it at first.

I wanted to seem like I had it figured out. The plan. The answers. The path.

Here's what I've learned:

Nobody has it figured out.

The people you admire most are not finished products.

They're just honest about being works in progress.

The need to appear polished is a trap.

It makes you rigid.
It makes you defensive.
It makes you afraid to start things you might be bad at.

And it quietly kills the growth it pretends to protect.

The alternative is simple:

Commit to getting better each day.

Not perfect. Better.

One conversation. One rep. One honest look in the mirror.

The people who grow the fastest are the ones who stopped pretending they didn't need to.

Fall in love with your unfinished form.

Trust where it leads.

——

Emotional control is the ultimate power.

(Few people actually have it.)

I'm convinced of this:

The ability to remain unshaken by the minor inconveniences of life puts you ahead of 95% of people.

Traffic.
A rude email.
Someone cutting in line.
A comment that stings for half a second.

Not every collision or slight deserves your energy.

You can just let them float by.

Protect your peace. Save your fire for what actually matters.

I think I'm having a Reverse Midlife Crisis.

(And I couldn't be happier about it.)

A few weeks ago, a friend said something at dinner that caught me off guard.

"I think I'm having a midlife crisis."

He's married with two kids.
He lives in the suburbs outside New York and commutes into the city for work.

Good job. Good family. Good life.
In many ways, the archetype of the dream.

But he'd been growing jealous of younger colleagues' freedom.
Scrolling Instagram, his feed filled with a life he felt he was running out of time to live.

In my view, the midlife crisis isn't driven by ego, vanity, or lust so much as fear.

Fear of a door permanently closed.
Fear of a road not taken.
Fear of a season past.

As I reflected on my own life, at a roughly similar stage, I had to be honest:

I think I'm having a Reverse Midlife Crisis.

A Midlife Crisis is about action that chases feelings from the past.
Re-living the things your 18-year-old self would find impressive.

Fast cars. Fancy stuff. Status symbols. Limited responsibilities.

A Reverse Midlife Crisis is about presence that compounds meaning for the future.
Building the things your 80-year-old self will find impressive.

Deep relationships. A healthy body. A grounded mind. Meaningful responsibilities.

Same fear.
Same anxiety.
Same grief over time lost.

The only difference is the direction of the response.

Don't cling to spring.
Stay interested in the changing seasons.

Swipe for the full story (and the three rules I'm living by).

——

Not every season needs to be your best.

(Some are just for surviving.)

The older I get, the more I realize that life has seasons.

Some seasons are for building.
Some are for healing.
Some are for just surviving.

You don't have to win every single chapter for the whole story to turn out well.

Here's what I've learned:

When you demand peak performance from a healing chapter, you punish yourself for doing the work that chapter actually requires.

Honor the season you're in.

Stop forcing a highlight reel out of a rebuild.

Your feelings are temporary.

(Your decisions often aren't.)

We've all been there.

Messages sent you can't take back. 
Calls made you spent years undoing.

You can always act tomorrow.
You can't always undo a rushed decision made today.

Learn to wait one more beat.

I noticed this in Mumbai during an ad shoot.
14 hours straight, 7 am to 9 pm, a team of about 200 people.

It wasn't my first shoot. 
But each one teaches me something.

This time I realised - to the experts on that set, I was not Ankur Warikoo. 
Not an actor, not a personal brand, not even a person.
I was whatever their craft needed me to be.

The moment I reached my hotel, the styling team was waiting. 
In 60 minutes, I wore 30+ outfits as they clicked away. 
To them, I was a mannequin.

To the makeup artist, a face. 
To the hairstylist, strands of hair. 
To the audio person, a voice. 
To the photographer, a model under lights. 
To the director, someone to emote.

Each of them had one task. 
And they executed it perfectly, without emotion, with exceptional skill.

It reminded me of the Mahabharata.

Dronacharya sets a bird's eye as the archery target and asks each student, "What do you see?"

One sees the tree. 
One the sky. 
One the whole bird.

Then comes Arjun. 
"What do you see, Arjun?"

"I see only the bird's eye, gurudev."

That is the difference between winners and losers.

Losers scan every possibility, and still miss.
Winners see only the mark.

How much of our life do we push to "when I"?

When I make money, I will be happy.
When I get the job, I will feel settled.
When I find a partner, I won't feel lonely.
When I clear that interview, everything will be okay.
When I have enough, I will start investing.

But here's the truth we keep missing.

If you aren't happy with the small things you already have, you will never be happy with the big things. 
Even if you get them.

The job won't fix it. 
The money won't fix it. 
The partner won't fix it.

Because happiness is not a destination.
It's a choice.

10 years ago, while raising money for my previous startup, an investor gave me the best money advice I've ever received -

"Money is not colorless. Money has color. And you have to decide which color of money you want to receive or give."

Here's what he meant.

Early in life, money is colourless. 

100 rupees is 100 rupees. 
We're just happy to receive it, whether we earned it or found it in an old jeans pocket.

But as you grow, you start to see the colour.

The same 10,000 earned at two different jobs isn't the same. 
One makes you proud. 
The other makes you miserable.

The same 10,000 spent isn't the same. 
One becomes a lifelong memory.
The other is just performative.

The same 10,000 invested isn't the same. 
One feels like a warm hug. 
The other has you addicted to swiping down and refreshing the screen.

That is the colour of money.

It shows up in the job you take. 
The same salary feels different depending on the values of the company, the leadership, the culture.

It shows up in the clients you work with. 
The same income feels different depending on how they treat you and the stress you wake up with.

Money isn't colourless.

It has shades. 
It has emotions. 
It has personality.

You have to choose which one you want to be friends with.

During a 1:1, a team member told me he has given up on love.

He is 25. 
I told him that's far too early to close that door.

He met his last girlfriend as a teenager. 
That was young love. 

And young love lives almost entirely on the surface. 
Looks, fashion, confidence, vibe, popularity. 
That's our selection criteria at 18.

Then reality arrives. 
We start seeing the true nature of the other person, while coming to terms with our own.

The biggest mistake we make is ignoring the obvious red flags. 
Because we're in love, and that's exactly what love does to us.

But at 25, young love is meant to grow into mature love.

You may still not know exactly who you're looking for. 
But you should be mature enough not to ignore the red flags this time.

You know better now than to fall only for a face. 
Fall for the mind too.

Because in the end, you will live with your partner's mind. 
Not their face.

As we grow and change, so does what love means to us. 
What you seek at 25 should look nothing like what you sought at 18.

So don't give up on love.
Give it a wiser chance.

30 min of reading, every day. 
For 15 years.

45 min workout, every day. 
For 12 years.

100+ days of travel, every year. 
For 5 years.

None of it was extraordinary on any single day.

All of it became extraordinary over time.

Consistency beats everything.

I have meditated every single day for over ~7yrs now.

Not because it's spiritual.

Because it gives me a 30-minute gap between a thought and my reaction to it.

That gap is worth more than any productivity hack I have ever tried.

Meditation didn't make me calmer in the moment. 
It did something better.

It put a pause between what happens to me and how I choose to respond to it.

Most of the damage in our lives happens in that tiny gap. 
When there is no gap.

We react. 
We snap. 
We send the message. 
We make the call. 
We say the thing.

And then we spend days cleaning up what a single un-paused moment created.

30 minutes a day buys me that pause.

It is the best trade I have ever made.

Recently, a 22-year-old commented:
"I don't use AI because it makes up facts, and then I have to spend time checking everything myself."

Also recently:
I got an AI tool to draft appraisal emails for my entire team. 
Based on each person's performance across the year. 
Within the budget I set. 
Personalising the feedback to a degree that felt eerily like me, drawn from our interactions all year.

The world used to be split between the haves and the have-nots.

Today it is split between the "don't want to" and the "want to."

The tools are sitting right there, free or nearly free, for everyone.
The only thing separating people now is willingness.

Crazy times.

5 one-month challenges that can change your life:
(Save this for progress!)

1. The communication challenge.

For the next 30 days, record yourself for one minute. 
Watch the video. Note down the mistakes. 
The next day, try to improve them.

2. The ‘saying no’ challenge. 

The things you often say yes to - to your boss, your parents, your friends - slowly practice saying no.

For 30 days, say no at least once every day in a situation where you used to say yes.

3. The decision-making challenge.

Whenever you have to make an important decision, give yourself a 10-minute timer. 
You must take a decision in 10 minutes.

Within 30 days, your capacity to take decisions under pressure will increase.

4. The negotiation challenge.

At least once a week, ask for a better deal. Negotiate. Ask for a better price.

In the beginning, you face humiliation. 
It feels very awkward. 
By the 30th day, you have a lot more confidence.

5. The structured thinking challenge.

Whenever you think about a problem, write it down. 
Break it down.

With small problems, the more you do that, the more structure enters the way you think.

Which one are you starting today?

5 money rules my wife and I follow as a couple aged 45 with two kids.

1. We don’t spend money to look rich. 

We spend to become wealthy and gain freedom of our time.

So, there’s no car. It’s rented. 
We own the house we live in, no other real estate.

No spending on brands. No spending just to show off to people.

2. We spend extravagantly on high-quality food.

We know that what goes into our body is ultimately the biggest wealth we have, and unfortunately, healthy food is not cheap.

3. We spend on experiences more than things.

Things give you happiness once, and they have no end.

You remember experiences, and they make you a better person. 
You grow as a person.

We travelled 116 days last year!

4. We invest before spending.

As soon as our salary comes, the largest amount is invested.

The remaining amount is used for expenses.

We are recording this on the 30th. 
₹9,000 and ₹600 left in our bank accounts. 
Everything else is invested.

5. No budget for books and learning.

No amount of money spent is enough.

Ruchi is learning pottery, watercolor painting, and tennis.

Our kids also go to many classes.

These are our rules. 
They may not apply to you, but having your own rules is important in life.

Before you say yes to marriage, check these 5 things.

1. Why are you getting married? Is it for the sake of society? Is it for the sake of your parents? Is it for your own good?

2. How do you handle fights with your partner? Because fights will continue. If you handle them properly, then relationships will progress.

3. Do you have an alignment on money and responsibility? How will you spend money? How will you share responsibilities?

4. Do you have space for your own personality? You can make friends without involving their friends. You can live your own life without depending on them.

5. How will you spend your life after marriage? What are the expectations from your family? How will your daily routines be? What will be your living arrangements? What have you thought about your children?

This is an important decision. Don't take it in a hurry.

Clear any interview with this 5-day challenge.

On Day 1 - prepare your 90-second introduction.

You have to focus on 4 things:
What are you doing right now?
What relevant experience do you have?
What are the things you are really good at?
And what do you want to do next?

Day 2 - design your proof.

This is all the evidence you can show a recruiter if they need any proof - proof of your work, internships, experience, and knowledge too.

Day 3 - practice stress interviews.

Pick your most powerful, strongest story or strength. Put it into ChatGPT and tell it to ask you follow-up stress questions. Answer them without preparing.

Day 4 - learn to answer a question whose answer you don’t know.

Upload your resume to ChatGPT and ask it to pose 30 questions that are not obvious, very difficult, and almost out of syllabus, and try to answer all of them.

Day 5 - do a 20-minute mock interview.

Activate ChatGPT voice and tell it your full context, and then say, “Take an interview in English.”

This 5-day training and preparation can help you prepare for every interview.

We grow up believing our parents are meant to have all the answers.

So when they get something wrong, we hold it against them for years.

But they were figuring out life for the first time too. 
With their own fears, their own wounds, their own parents they were still healing from.

They were never perfect beings.

They were just people, doing their best with what they knew at the time.

The day you start seeing your parents as humans first, a lot of your anger quietly turns into understanding.
The numbers in these 4 movies will shock you!

If a friend or relative asks you for money, how do you handle it without making things awkward?

These 5 rules can help.

1/ Never lend more than you are comfortable losing.

2/ If you can give the money, don’t treat it as a loan. 
Tell yourself, “If I get it back, that’s great, but I assume this money won’t come back.”

3/ If you cannot lend the money, say so directly. 
If you beat around the bush, it will make things awkward.

4/ For large amounts, always put it in writing.

5/ Never lend money again to someone who hasn’t returned it the first time.

But someone who kept learning might.

A girl went to college and forgot her parents. 
After many days, she wrote them a letter:

“Maa, Papa, before you read this, I want you to sit down. I wanted to tell you that as soon as I went to college, my room caught fire. 

I had to jump out of my window to save my life. 

God bless the boy who came running and saved my life. 
He would come to see me in the hospital. 
We became friends and I don’t know when that friendship turned into love. 

Now, we are married. 
There was no hurry, but my pregnancy is visible now. 
And I didn’t want it to show at the wedding.

Maa, Papa, please listen carefully. 

There was no fire, I don’t have a boyfriend, I am not pregnant, and whatever I said was not true. 

I just failed all my exams.”

Now, see how quickly this letter changed. 
But why? 

Because perspective is everything. 

If the daughter straight away told them that she failed, then that wouldn’t have worked. 

But suddenly, seeing all these things, the parents would have said, “You just failed. 
No problem, work harder next time.” 

Perspective changes everything!
Share this with someone who would find this helpful.

experience.description:
Voices of Rural India is a not-for-profit digital initiative to host curated stories by rural storytellers, in their own voices. 

The Covid-19 induced lockdown has brought India’s tourism industry to a grinding halt. Rural communities have lost their livelihoods, supply chains have been disrupted and alternate income streams have thinned.

Voices of Rural India is an effort to turn this unprecedented crisis into an opportunity to create alternate livelihoods by upgrading digital skills in rural India, while also preserving grassroots knowledge that is slowly disappearing.

In the short-term, Voices of Rural India aims to create a revenue stream for affected communities through digital journalism. It will help develop digital storytelling skills using basic tools at the grassroots level, with a focus on women and the youth.

In the long run, Voices of Rural India aims to become a repository of oral traditions, local folklore and the culture of rural India, documented in local voices. The digital skills thus acquired can be used to support rural entrepreneurship ventures.

For the rest of us, stuck at home, this is a chance to explore remote corners of India through the stories of the very people we travel to meet.

The recent devastating Nepal floods highlight the dire need for climate justice - and I'm surprised hardly any media publications, climate podcasts and climate newsletters are talking about it.
 
👉 Last month, a Himalayan glacier collapsed, leading to one of the biggest flash floods the region has witnessed. It wiped out entire homes, schools and communities from a high mountain valley in Nepal. ~1400 people lost their lives; 6000+ are still missing.
 
👉 For decades, scientists have warned that the Hindu Kush Himalayas - aka the Third Pole (the third biggest frozen water reserve after the North and South Poles) - have been warming at nearly double the global average.

The region’s glaciers are melting. Snowfall patterns are unpredictable. River flows are changing. Leading to glacial lake outbursts floods and mountain avalanches that are deeply affect local communities, their lives, livelihoods and ecosystems.
 
👉 Despite global discussions to reduce GHG emissions, we continue to burn fossil fuels, use forest land for animal agriculture, destroy carbon sinks like mangroves and wetlands, overfish our oceans, and create more climate-warming gases than can be absorbed. Historically, countries in the Global North have been the highest emitters - as they industrialized their countries, extracted resources from the Global South, and grew their economies.

They are also facing the consequences of climate change but not in the same way. Their economic conditions allow them to shield citizens from the worst impacts. When a recent glacial collapse happened in Switzerland, advanced weather warning systems allowed the entire village to be evacuated. No lives lost.
 
👉 A country like Nepal has contributed less than 0.01% of global climate emissions. But like many countries in the Global South, it bears the unfair burden of climate impacts. The Third Pole has 63000+ glaciers and many of them are not monitored. There is no finance or technological transfer to adapt to the changing climate.
 
Climate adaptation is absolutely necessary because even if we cut emissions globally now (which we are not on track to do), the carbon already in the atmosphere will continue to create impacts for years to come.
 
👉 For years, the Global South - from Himalayan nations to small island states – has demanded that the highest historical emitters pay damage and adaptation costs to those that bear the biggest impacts. Not loans and investments that grab land, but finance and technology transfer so more lives don’t have to be lost to climate disasters like in Nepal. So far, these negotiations have been in vain.
 
👉 This is why we need climate justice. As carbon emissions continue to grow and global planetary temperatures rise, climate justice is ensuring that no one unfairly bears the burden of climate impacts.

#Nepalfloods #climatejustice #climatecommunication

Today marks 100 consecutive days of the Flamingo Revolution in Albania. On day 98, I witnessed it on the streets of Tirana. 

👉🏼 Unlike much of Europe, Albania is still home to old growth forests (never destroyed in its tumultuous history) and rich coastal natural resources. The protests began when the government quietly built an airport next to a protected area, with the aim of diluting its protected status for luxury tourism development. 

👉🏼 The night I joined the protest, hundreds of Albanians were out on the streets, proclaiming that Albania is not for sale. At the height of the protests, ~300,000 people from across the country and the diaspora took to the streets - the largest protest since the fall of communism. 

👉🏼 A young Albanian woman told me that she’s never in her lifetime, seen people come together like this, irrespective of party or politics, for the collective cause of protecting nature, fighting corruption and keeping public access to protected areas. 

👉🏼 Albanians who work in tourism are at the frontlines of the revolution, because this is not the kind of tourism they want. They don’t want tourism that sells off protected areas to rich outsiders, excludes locals from accessing their public lands, extracts long-conserved natural resources especially now in the face of climate change, and economically benefits only a select few. 

👉🏼 Over the two weeks I spent in northern Albania, I witnessed both - how tourism can enable local communities and living cultures to thrive, and how it can bring economic benefits at the cost of local ways of life. More on that soon, but I hope this revolution leads to solutions that centre people and the planet, not just profit.  

#albania #flamingorevolution #slowtravel #balkans #sustainabletourism #regenerativetravel

I think writing a book is one of the most solitary things a human can do. 

I found myself traversing parts of my mind and memories only known to me. I dug within for words and emotions I wanted on the page. It was me, my notebook, my laptop, my paper scraps and my printed manuscript for so long.

I had no choice but to let go of the book when I sent the final draft to my editor at Penguin. When time came to launch it several months later, I felt like I was already a whole other person than the one who wrote it. It felt surreal to dive into its stories again, this time from the perspective of readers. I felt a strange déjà vu trying to access the version of me who wrote those 352 pages!

But I think what came as a great surprise, in this era of diminishing attention spans, is the attention to detail. 

During the first leg of my book tour in India, I was floored by the kind of questions readers asked - about the book, the places I wrote about, the themes I touch upon, the act of writing, the desire to navigate the world as an Indian woman and the uncomfortable paradoxes of travel. My current home base - Berlin - hit a record-breaking ~40°C in Europe’s recent heatwave! Just four months before that, we were at -15°C. 

Berlin, like most European cities, is built for the cold. Buildings are designed to trap heat, most apartments (including ours) don’t come with fans or ACs, public transport is not air-conditioned. 

As I hid out the heatwave at home, in parks and even cinema halls (yes!), I couldn't help but research how cities around the world are adapting, and solutions that could work for many European cities:

👉 Repurpose public infrastructure into cooling shelters 

Incheon has been turning subway stations, gyms, exhibition halls and other public infrastructure into cooling shelters. Cooling fog systems and mobile water sprinklers are installed at busy walkways, bus shelters and exposed walking pavements.
 
👉 Create heat relief maps and apps for cities

Paris has created an app with a list of 800 ‘cool islands’ across the city – including water fountains, swimming pools and forests – connected by shaded walkways. Its climate adaptation plan aims to have a cool island within 7 minutes of each resident.

Incheon has been sharing heat relief guides through TV, radio and social media.

👉 Train ‘heatwave helpers’ for residents in need

Incheon has trained ~7000 volunteers to assist during heatwaves. They check in with senior citizens, offer first aid and can help call for additional help.

👉 Create green corridors to reduce urban temperatures

Medellin has reduced urban summer temperatures by 2°C by creating green corridors that mimic natural forests and reduce heat through evapotranspiration - adding water vapour in the air. 

👉 Summer-proof residential and office buildings 
 
People in France have been using DIY chalk paint on windows to reflect heat – and now run low on chalk stock! European cities can mandate installation of external blinds across residential and office buildings.

👉 Mandate green facades on buildings

Concrete jungles within cities create heat traps by absorbing and emitting heat, especially in the summer. A building in Düsseldorf has installed Europe’s largest green façade (8 km of green roof + vertical garden) which protect the building against the strong sun and reduce the heat island effect.

Which of these strategies do you think could benefit your city?

#europe #heatwaves #climateadaptation #berlin #climatechange
