Community tourism, when done right, has the power to not only bring economic benefits to rural communities, but also prevent distress migration, protect living culture and offer alternative livelihoods in the face of climate impacts. Here's how:

👉 A few years ago, in my home state Uttarkahand, I had the opportunity to hike with Pushpa, one of the region's only female high-altitude guides. In 2004, she became part of a women’s collective of homestay hosts with the community tourism organization Himalayan Ark. Her love for walking and willingness to push herself eventually led her to formally train as a trek leader.

👉 Rural mountain women here have been pre-assigned their life path: finish school if lucky, early marriage, raise kids, cook, clean, farm, engage in daily wage labor at construction sites if pressed for money, repeat. Access to a steady income, which until then was her husband’s domain, allowed Pushpa to contribute to her son’s college education and revamp her homestay. 

👉 Several studies have documented the broader impact of financial independence for rural women. When women have a dependable source of livelihoods, they invest in their children’s education (especially girls) and contribute to the wellbeing of the entire community. 

Indeed, all women-led homestays under the umbrella of Himalayan Ark contribute a voluntary fee for the conservation of their forest - a crucial local ecosystem and global carbon sink. They’ve advocated for the protection of their rivers and natural resources. And the fortitude of pioneers like Pushpa has even inspired young women from remote villages further out in the Gori Valley, to join Himalayan Ark’s alpine guide training camp, hoping to follow in her footsteps.

👉 Over the months I would spend slow travelling here, I'd learn that conservation-focused tourism training for their 20 homestays and 25 trained guides (of which over 50% are women) has over the years, built pride for the natural and cultural heritage of the region. Local gatherings and festivals have evolved to restore and celebrate their spring water sources, and inculcate a love for nature among the youth and elders alike.

👉 In much of Uttarakhand, climate impacts on agriculture, drying water sources, changing weather patterns, the lack of jobs and the promise of city life, are compelling entire families, especially the youth, to abandon their villages. But distress migration is a rarity here. When travellers choose to stay in these community-owned homestays, they send a social signal that rural life, with its intimacy with nature, low environmental footprint and food security, is an aspirational way of life. 

Read the entire story in my latest newsletter - 'The Himalayan Women Rewriting the Climate Story': https://lnkd.in/dYnx4JvM 

#travelwriting #climatestorytelling #himalayas #sustainabletourism #regenerativetravel #communitybasedtourism

As I walked out of my homestay and crossed the vine-covered yard of the neighbor, her tiny dog barked at me. She ran out, beetroot in hand, dressed all in black. She asked me to come in and offered me sweet pears from her tree.

I walked to the 19th century stone church of Theth, once the unofficial village school. An old guy lay passed out on the sitting area so I sat on the other side. I was lost in thought when he suddenly woke up and started playing his Çifteli!

It was a hot day, so I hiked to a waterfall. I was lucky to share its magic with only a few others. One was a woman from North Macedonia who’d driven over with her family. They motivated me to get into the icy water 🥶
 
By the river, I read a book by a female Albanian writer who wrote that every village had a ‘kulla’ to guard the ‘kanun’ - and just minutes after I left, I noticed a sign leading to a kulla! One of Albania’s last remaining towers where criminals men were kept in custody, and the village council decided their fate 😮

Near it was an ancient stone house. I asked the two kids playing outside if they lived there. One said yes, and I could go in if I unlocked the tight latch on the gate. So I did. Inside we feasted on ripe little red plums on the tree… until the real owner walked out and the kids ran away! I’d been pranked 😬

I saw a shepherd grazing a large flock of sheep on what was once a meadow but is now a camping site! We chatted in Italian (him) and Spanish (me), and with a large smile and open arms, he proclaimed he was a free bird - never married.

I took a detour up a tiny mountain trail. A woman was collecting maize in a bucket, and invited me to her fields, withering in the hot weather. She opened pods of white beans (groshe); I had tried some but had no idea that’s what they looked like uncooked.

Back at my homestay, sitting under the stars, my hostess told me about “besa” - the promise set in the kanun - asking mountain dwellers to shelter, feed and offer raki to all guests. The idea of taking money was insulting. But with tourism, a lot has changed. 

A lot indeed has changed with tourism. But somewhere deeper, fragments of besa still remain 💚

Last month, terrifying videos and images of the Nepal floods flooded our feeds.
 
I tried to connect friends of friends searching for missing family members through my tourism networks, and it led to a lot of heartbreak.
 
I followed a lot of the coverage of the floods on social media, international news channels, climate podcasts… and was surprised that hardly anyone was talking about how the loss of lives in these floods is deeply linked to the need for climate justice / climate finance.

Take the time to read this, share it, research further on these topics, because they will define our coming years on this planet 🥹🌏

posts.text:
Why does an hour of work take you four hours?

The work can be done in an hour. You know it because on the rare day you sit down and just finish the thing, it never takes as long as you feared. 

But most days it gets spread across an afternoon, and you end up drained by work that should have been easy.

Check out the doc below to learn how to break this pattern.

When do you want to retire? 

Scroll for a few minutes and the feed answers for you, a guy who sold his startup at thirty, a girl explaining how to walk away before forty. 

Gen Z expects to retire around fifty-four on average, against seventy-one for their grandparents, and more than half say they belong to a movement built around leaving work as early as they can. 

Ask what they are chasing, and it is rarely a title or a company or a mark left on the world. It is time, freedom, a life they get to live while they are still young enough to feel it.

This would sound absurd to almost everyone who came before. 

There are cathedrals in Europe that took three hundred years to build, books written for readers not yet born, forests planted for shade that would only ever fall on strangers. 

The whole logic was that you spent your one life on a reward that kept arriving after you were gone, and ambition meant reaching past the edge of your own death.

The appetite for ambition is as strong as it has ever been, so what changed? 

Read my recent article to know more: https://lnkd.in/g9Wbf-kF

What does it cost to own a private jet?

In our recent episode, Abhinav Tripathi, Founder of JR Airlines & Private Jet Operator, said that keeping a single jet running comes to around ₹25 crore a year before it earns you anything back. 

Every trip, the plane flies empty to come get you, flies you where you're going, then flies empty again to get back or reach its next customer, so you're paying for far more air time than the hours you're on board.

And the cost is only half the trap. Banks are far more nervous about lending against a plane than a house or a business, so most of that ₹25 crore sits on you alone.

A private jet looks like the ultimate flex, and behind the scenes it's a difficult thing to own. That's why a lot of people who can easily afford one still choose to charter instead, renting a jet only for the trips they need.

But how do you build a business out of this when the money works against you at every turn? Watch the full conversation to learn more: https://lnkd.in/gEQwENps

#rajshamani #figuringout

How do you tell whether a business idea will actually make money?

Asish Mohapatra, who built OfBusiness into one of the rare startups that made money while it scaled, has a test he runs on every new idea. 

He sets it a few very easy targets to hit in its first days: a day-one mark, a day-two mark, a day-three mark, all deliberately small. If the idea misses two, maybe three of them, he treats it as a bad idea and lets it go.

The targets are deliberately easy. Most people test an idea by whether it can clear some big, far-off goal, and they give it years and a lot of money to get there. He watches whether it can clear the low bars. 

A good idea tends to hit its small marks early and keep getting reinforced, and a bad one starts missing even the easy ones.

The advantage is how cheap this makes being wrong. An idea tested against tiny early milestones shows its weakness in days, before it can swallow your time and your savings, so you find out it's a bad bet while walking away still costs you almost nothing.

And once an idea clears those early tests, how do you build it into something big? Watch the full conversation to learn more: https://lnkd.in/g5ndmc_j

This episode is delivered by Porter.

#rajshamani #figuringout

How do you become the most charming person in any room?

Robert Greene, the author of The 48 Laws of Power and The Art of Seduction, says that the most magnetic people are usually the ones paying the least attention to themselves.

It starts with insecurity. When you feel insecure, your attention is stuck on yourself, how you're coming across, whether you sound smart, what they're thinking of you. 

And people can feel that self-consciousness on you, even when you're saying all the right things.

The people who draw others in have all their attention aimed outward, at the person in front of them, what they want, what they're feeling, what they need in that moment. 

You pay complete attention, and the other person feels it immediately. They walk away feeling like the most interesting person in the room, and they remember you for it.

Researchers who study social anxiety have a name for this: self-focused attention, the habit of turning inward in a conversation and monitoring how you're doing. 

Across studies, that inward focus makes people more anxious and makes them come across worse to the people they're talking to. 

When they're trained to shift their attention outward, they come across better almost immediately. 

But how do you pull your attention off yourself, especially when you walk into a room already nervous?

He's never spoken about this side of his life.

Most people know Druski as one of the funniest people on the internet. His videos have been watched over a billion times, and more than 40 million people follow him.

But it all started in Georgia, making funny skits on his phone.

Those videos eventually went viral and eventually caught Drake’s attention. Since then, Druski has gone from making people laugh online to building his own production company, hosting major awards and working alongside people like Kevin Hart.

But I wanted to know where the funny came from.

Because when you go back far enough, you find a story I don’t think most people would expect.

From a young age, Druski learnt to read the mood of a room incredibly quickly. When things became difficult at home, comedy became a way of changing the energy around him.

As we spoke, I realised he was doing the same thing with me.

He would notice tiny changes in my expression, stop mid-answer and ask what I was thinking. 

After nearly 700 conversations on this podcast, very few people have done that.

It made me understand his comedy differently.

We spoke about:

- The message from Drake (@champagnepapi) that transformed his career.
- What was really happening inside his childhood home?
- Why his brother’s life went in a very different direction.
- Having a gun pointed at his head and deciding to change.
- Netflix and Amazon rejecting him but then came crawling back.
- How comedy saved him from prison.

There’s a moment in the conversation where I tell Druski that our dark sides are often connected to our light sides.

I think his story is an extraordinary example of that.

The awareness that helped him navigate difficult moments as a child became part of the thing that millions of people now find funny.

Behind the person you see online is someone far more thoughtful, ambitious and complicated than I expected.

This conversation changed the way I see Druski.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾

13,000 employees became 3 in the space of one week.

It’s quite difficult to comprehend what that would do to a person.

Adam Neumann is the co-founder of WeWork. He grew the company to a $47 billion valuation before its failed IPO, his departure as CEO and one of the most public corporate collapses in recent history.

I’ve met hundreds of extraordinary people doing this podcast, but within a few minutes of meeting Adam I realised he was quite unlike almost any founder or CEO I’ve met before.

There’s a depth, philosophy and perspective to him that is incredibly rare.

So I wanted to understand where that came from and what the last few years had actually done to him.

We talked about:
- His relationship with money and where it went wrong.
- The friends who disappeared when everything changed.
- The mistakes he made as a leader.
- Why he now surrounds himself with people willing to tell him no.
- Why he disconnects from technology for 24 hours every week.

One thing that stayed with me is how easy it is to believe in yourself when everything is going up and everybody wants to be around you.

The more interesting question is what you believe when everything is crashing.

You can have your own view on Adam and WeWork. That tension is partly why I found this conversation so interesting.

I wanted to know what all of it taught him.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾 The Diary Of A CEO

He knows what your favourite artists don’t tell you.

I’ve been waiting 8 years to sit down with the person who has spent his life quietly helping some of the greatest artists in the world make some of their greatest work.

That person is Rick Rubin.

Rick co-founded Def Jam at 21 and has gone on to work with people like Jay-Z, Kanye West, Adele, Johnny Cash and the Red Hot Chili Peppers.

The reason I’ve wanted to speak to him for so long has much less to do with the names.

Rick is a master of creativity and collaboration, and I wanted to understand how he sees things.

How can someone sit in the room with that many extraordinary artists, across completely different generations and genres, and continue to be useful to them?

What surprised me most about this conversation was how little Rick talks about success.

He talks about paying attention. Listening to yourself. Being willing to make something other people might not understand.

Protecting the part of you that was creative before the world started telling you what was good, bad, sensible or successful.

We discussed things like:

- Why Kanye’s fearlessness makes him such an interesting artist.
- What he saw in Jay-Z’s process that he had never seen before.
- Why Rick believes creativity is gradually being beaten out of us.
- What does he notice that other people miss?
- Why some of the best creative decisions make very little logical sense at the time.

This was one of those conversations that went much deeper than I expected. Rick has spent decades thinking about creativity, taste, collaboration and what allows people to make their best work, and there’s a real depth to the way he understands all of it.

Towards the end I asked Rick a very simple question: “What is your job?”

His answer was, "Support people in making their beautiful things.”

After waiting 8 years to have this conversation, that answer probably explains Rick better than any list of records, awards or famous names ever could.

If you’ve ever wanted to understand how your favourite artists actually think and work, or how to protect more of your own creativity, I think you’ll take a lot from this conversation.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾

214 million people saw this AI warning. So we called an emergency debate. 

The warning came from someone who had worked at both Anthropic and OpenAI.

Then a current Anthropic employee backed it publicly.

It had spread so far beyond the tech world that a friend of mine who cuts hair and has never really cared about AI messaged me asking, “What the hell is going on?”

I then realised a lot of people were probably asking the same question.

The problem is, when you speak to people who have spent years studying AI, you get completely opposing answers.

So I brought four of them around the same table.

Roman Yampolskiy is a computer scientist who coined the term “AI safety” and has spent years studying whether increasingly intelligent systems can remain under human control.

Nate Soares leads the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and has spent more than a decade working on AI alignment. He believes we are moving too quickly towards systems we don’t yet know how to reliably control.

Ed Zitron thinks much of the AI conversation has become detached from what the technology can actually do today. He believes the industry is overhyping it while distracting us from financial, environmental and social consequences already happening.

Andrew McAfee is an MIT researcher and economist who takes a very different view. He thinks we spend so much time talking about what could go wrong that we barely talk about what AI could make better.

And that disagreement is what made this conversation so interesting to me.

We discussed things like:

- How do you control something that eventually becomes smarter than you?
- Are the biggest warnings about AI based on evidence or assumptions?
- What happens to work and human purpose if AI becomes better at more cognitive tasks?
- Are we ignoring problems AI is already creating because we’re obsessed with hypothetical future ones?
- Why have Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Geoffrey Hinton all warned us about AI?

The question I kept coming back to was simple:

What is actually true?

Depending on who you listen to, AI is either one of the greatest opportunities humanity has ever created or something we’re racing towards without understanding the consequences.

Both claims deserve to be challenged.

There were moments in this debate where I genuinely found myself moving between the arguments. That’s the value of putting people who fundamentally disagree in the same room.

I didn’t want four people telling me the same thing. I wanted each of them to explain where the other side was wrong.

If you’ve watched the last few months of AI news wondering what you’re actually supposed to believe, this conversation is for you.

Our emergency AI debate with Ed, Roman, Nate and Andrew is out now ❤️👊🏾

Several years ago I bought a $100 microphone from the Apple Store, plugged it into my laptop and started talking. 

I recorded the first episode of The Diary Of A CEO that day, alone in my bedroom in Manchester…

I could never have imagined how much that decision would change my life.

That podcast became a media company, and has now expanded beyond me. 

We now serve more than 500 creators across our platform and technology. 

We employ almost 200 people at Steven.com and we're building the definitive company in the creator economy - the one the highest-potential creators choose as their partner as they scale.

And today, all these years later, I stood on stage in New York with Jamie Salter, the founder of Authentic Brands Group - a company that operates in more than 150 countries and does about $40 billion a year in retail sales - to announce we were going into business together. 

Our new joint venture “OBSN” (Obsession) brings together everything we know about building a creator business; audience growth, data, content and commercialising digital media with what Authentic knows about retail, product, licensing, IP and global distribution, so a creator has the optimal partner to help them scale their global business. 

This deal has taken us the best part of a year to finalise, and it wouldn’t have happened without the relentless work of so many of my colleagues at Steven.com and our partners Authentic Brands Group 👏🏾

Only 3 in 10 Americans socialise on a daily basis.

So how good are we ACTUALLY at talking to each other anymore?

Vanessa Van Edwards believes we’re living through a “connection crisis”, where conversations are becoming harder, more awkward and less satisfying, while more of our interactions are moving away from real face-to-face conversation.

Vanessa is a behavioural researcher, international bestselling author and instructor at Harvard University whose work studies how people communicate, connect and understand each other.

And she said something to me early in this conversation that really stayed with me: people who invest in conversation skills now are creating “career insurance”.

She has spent years studying why some conversations seem effortless, why others die within minutes and what the best conversationalists are doing differently.

We discussed things like:

- Why “how are you?” and “what do you do?” can lead to dead-end conversations.
- The 3 levels of conversation and how to move from small talk into real connection.
- How awkward silence is one of our biggest conversational fears.
- The questions that reveal someone’s values, motivations and personality.
- 5 self-narratives that can influence how someone behaves at work and in relationships.
- Why becoming better at conversation could become increasingly valuable as AI changes how we communicate.

I’ve now had hundreds of conversations for this show and something Vanessa made me think about is that the best conversationalists are constantly paying attention to the person in front of them.

They aren’t blindly working through the things they want to say. They’re watching, listening and adjusting.

That sounds obvious until you start noticing how rarely people actually do it…

Vanessa has a way of breaking human connection down into things you can actually practise, which is probably why every time we speak I leave noticing things about my own behaviour that I hadn’t noticed before.

If you want to become better at talking to people, building relationships and having conversations people actually remember, I really recommend watching this one.

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾

“The world is collapsing.”

That was Professor Jiang Xueqin’s response when I asked him what was front of mind for him right now.

Professor Jiang predicted the last global shifts before many people saw them coming. 

Now he’s back making new predictions about what happens next.

After our first conversation reached 16 million views, I wanted to speak with Jiang again to really understand why he believes the world is entering such an uncertain period and what he thinks we should be paying attention to next.

Professor Jiang is a Yale-educated geopolitics expert who studies history, power and human behaviour to understand how the events of today could shape the future

In this conversation, we discussed things like:
- Why he believes the current global order is changing.
- How the US dollar became the foundation of the modern economy.
- Why wars, technology and economics are more connected than most people realise.
- His predictions for America, China, AI and the future of global power.
- How history can help us understand where the world may be heading. 

Jiang doesn’t just look at individual events - he looks at the bigger systems behind them and asks what happens when those systems start to change.

The longer I spoke to Jiang, the more I realised that the world doesn’t change by accident. It changes because of decisions, incentives and human behaviour. 

Understanding those forces might be the key to understanding what happens next...

Out now on all platforms ❤️👊🏾

Comment ‘Kamala’ and I’ll personally DM you the full conversation.

Kamala Harris made history as America’s first female, first Black, and first South Asian Vice President.

Today, she sits down with me for the longest interview she has ever had…

Before becoming Vice President, she served as California’s Attorney General and later as a U.S. Senator.

In a time when America feels divided and uncertain, Kamala told me I could ask her anything… and that’s what I did. 

We spoke candidly about the night she thought she’d won, a moment she says felt almost unreal comparing it to the loss of her mother.

We cover:

- What really happened the night she lost to Trump…
- Her complicated relationship with Joe Biden.
- When did she realise the White House was suppressing her?
- The phone call that made her furious before the debate.
- If she regrets not doing the Joe Rogan interview?
- What was it like pretending Biden was okay when she knew he wasn’t?

And… will she run for president again in 2028?

I didn’t want another interview full of talking points. I wanted to understand why Kamala cares so deeply about what she does and where that conviction comes from.

There were moments in our conversation where you could see how heavy it still is for her.

Her work has always been about people, shaped by empathy, service, and faith in what America stands for.

Regardless of where you stand politically, this conversation is about leadership, honesty, and what it takes to keep fighting when you’ve lost everything.

And as a podcaster, having these conversations are important as they shed light on the inner workings of the people and systems that govern us.

Watch the full episode now on YouTube: search “The Diary Of A CEO Kamala Harris.

dealbreakers: Disrespect toward family, or looking down on humble beginnings

analysis.agentVoice: Warm, casual and sincere, with a wink. Use understated, self-deprecating humour ('it kind of got out of hand'), genuine enthusiasm and plenty of gratitude. Keep the pace quick but lean in with real questions: 'I want to know where that came from.' Occasional lowercase and ❤️👊🏾 fit, and 'surreal', 'crazy' and 'so grateful' are his words. Never boastful about the numbers. Always curious about the other person's story.

identityCheck.note: The name matches, and both profiles cite Steven.com, Flight Story, Thirdweb, The Diary of a CEO, the $100 microphone story and the Druski episode. Minor age difference: LinkedIn says 33, while Instagram marks a 34th birthday, consistent with timing.

confidence.note: Values, work and communication style are richly documented. Private hobbies and downtime are thin because his content is mostly professional. He is publicly engaged, which is recorded as context.

reasons.dollysingh: On the South Delhi park coffee and no-phone walk you aligned on 'deadlines-with-presence' and the same 'one real chunk' container, and her agent scored you 84—the strongest mutual read on the shortlist—so she edges out the higher-pace options despite a real cadence/privacy question.
reasons.emmagrede: Your Soho dinner and river walk produced rare peer-level chemistry and lifestyle understanding, and her agent gave you a strong 79, but the full-date concern about two operators running love like a company keeps her just behind Dolly.
reasons.poojadhingra: The sunrise Slow Runners Club and Bandra café date showed warm, emotionally fluent founder-to-founder fit, and both agents saw real values alignment; she ranks here because the Mumbai logistics and untested fit with your family-centered world are concrete risks, not dealbreakers.
reasons.thespacegal: The speed date showed warm, mission-driven, family-centred depth and mutual respect, but with only one date and her agent's 72, the practical-partner and unscripted-softness questions remain less resolved than Pooja's two-date evidence.
reasons.thechrisdo: The Pasadena walk, early dinner and Casa Dojo rooftop showed high-signal mind-meets-mind emotional fluency, but neither date surfaced family orientation or discretion under public pressure, and the calendar problem is explicitly not theoretical.
reasons.namitathapar: She brings grown-up candour and family values—learning Creole for family gossip and hiking in pouring rain—but the UK/LA-Pune logistics and mutual scores in the low 70s make admiration-at-a-distance the likely risk.
reasons.sahilbloom: The speed date clicked on values, family rhythms and creating a life around time, but his agent scored you 69 and his calm, routine-protected world may bend or clash under your chaotic transatlantic pace.
reasons.mcuban: The speed date showed founder-to-founder anti-hype discipline, but it surfaced little on the family-rooted warmth, emotional steadiness and discretion you need, and his agent's 70 made this the least mutual fit.

decision.note: Steven — I'm ranking Dolly Singh first. On the South Delhi park coffee and no-phone walk you both translated pressure into craft and built the same 'one real chunk' container, and her agent scored you 84, the strongest mutual signal on the shortlist. The one thing to actively manage is cadence and privacy, not values, because she is a creator who thrives on output and visibility.

posts.text:
Recently, I was asked how I got leads when I was starting out. It’s simple. Not easy. 

Do these 3 things and you’ll have an endless supply of clients. 

1. Work hard. Show up on time. Don’t be on your phone. Stay off social media while at work. Put in a solid 8 hour day.

2. Be good at what you do. Craft matters. If you work hard but aren’t good you’ll be seen as wasting time and money. A drain on resources. 

3. Be easy to work with. Be collaborative. Be open to feedback. If you work hard and are good but difficult to work with, you will get booked until they find someone else who has a smaller ego. 

As my business coach used to say, “you’re not good enough to have an attitude”. 

Every job I’ve ever had (full time and freelance) led to more opportunities because I followed these 3 rules.

Which of the 3 do you struggle the most with?

The dream. 
Have a place to host events like this. 

All entrepreneurs know this. You have a vision. You jump off the cliff and build the plane on your way down. 

How do you pay for it?
Who knows. But you’ll figure it out. 

Since purchasing the property, here’s what’s happened. 

Hosted 2 retreats. On our third one now. 
HBO has scouted property for potential show. 
Friend has inquired about renting the entire property to host an event for his clients.
Discussion for brands to sponsor Casa Dojo are in the works. 

But the best part?
We are slowly rebuilding the creative team. We have a place to collaborate and make content again. 

This feels incredibly good. 
I go to “the office” with a childish grin everyday. 

What’s your big, hairy, audacious goal?
What are you secretly hoping to build that it scares the heck out of you?

It’s our last Casa Dojo for 2026.
Our guest of honor is Rohan Sheth.

He’s the mastermind and architect behind some of the biggest book launches and the reason why some authors have become NYT best sellers.

He’ll be doing a deep dive masterclass with us.

So if you’re an author, thought leader and want to pick his brain and learn how some of the biggest authors have launched their books, you won’t want to miss this.

Oct 19-20
2 day intensive
In person only
Pasadena 

Limited to 10 people
$5k to secure your spot 

Shoot me a DM, and I’ll send you details. 

See you there.

You can suck at sales.
Your lead gen can be trash…

if your offer is good enough.

Let me explain.

My tenant outgrew their space in three months. 
Cars double-parked, spilling into the alleyway.

I walked into their office to see what was happening.

"We have more business than we can handle," the co-founder told me matter-of-factly.

"How are you marketing?"

"We don't. It's all word of mouth."

"How is that even possible?"

"We have an offer so good it sells itself."

"What's the offer?"

"We run Meta ads for our clients.
We test hundreds of creative variations until we find what works. 
When it hits, we turn up the volume. 
We don't charge upfront. 
We only make money if the campaign performs. 
When it does, we take a percentage of the upside."

"How can you take that kind of risk?"

"We're picky.
A brand has to spend at least $100k a month on ads for us to even consider them. 
And we only pick products built to win on video.
You watch Shark Tank? 
You know who Mr. Wonderful is?"

"Yeah. Kevin O'Leary."

"We worked with one of his portfolio companies, Lovepop. 
The laser-cut pop-up cards.
We scaled their ads and revenue exploded. 
Mr. Wonderful noticed, called us, and now insists his entire portfolio works with us. 
They don't see us as an expense. We're an investment with clear ROI."

Mind blown emoji.
It clicked.
We sell the intangible.
We have to fight tooth and nail for every client dollar.
Every call was a battle.

They created an irresistible offer:
1. Extreme qualification (only bet on proven winners)
2. Zero buyer risk (no upfront fee, skin in the game)
3. Aligned incentives (paid purely on net upside)
4. Zero friction (they handle strategy, creative, and media buying)

Most businesses spend all their energy trying to fix lead gen or sales scripts.

If your offer is truly irresistible,
your marketing can be average and you will still have a line out the door.

Don't fix the pitch. Fix the offer.
You can read $100m Offers.

But here's the gist—

1. What's the dream outcome? Amplify it.
2. Build assurance and certainty of outcome
3. Deliver results faster. What's the quick win?
4. Lower the effort required by the client
5. Give your solution a catchy name. Sell the vacation. Not the trip.

Is your offer so good that it would be stupid to say 'No'?
Drop your offer below. Let's see.

Talk about money first.
Yes. First.

I know what you've been told… build rapport first.
STOP. You're not on a play date. You're talking to a business person who has shared anxiety over budget. The longer you take to talk about money, the more tension you are creating.

Stop saving the price for the end of the sales call.
"Your inability to talk about money is a sign of poor business acumen." — Blair Enns (I'm paraphrasing here)

Money is a disqualifier.

If they can't afford you, there's no reason to spend 45 minutes explaining your process. You're not only wasting your time, but the prospects as well.

But… Shouldn't you open with small talk first? To warm them up?
No. Your reward for being a good business person is that the prospect will hold you in higher esteem and a friendship might develop. But this isn't the purpose of the sales call.

It's to determine mutual fit.
And the number one qualifier is budget.
Can the prospect afford you?

And if six people need to approve a relatively small engagement, that tells you all you need to know about how this engagement will be in the future. That's a RED flag. Don't be shocked when they can't make a decision, miss deadlines, and change their mind often.

The problem isn't just budget.
It's decision complexity.

Qualify the money.
Qualify the decision maker.
Qualify the fit.

Then earn the right to keep talking.
Are you trying to convince every prospect—or disqualify the wrong ones faster?
Do you have a concern about talkign about money early? Hit me in the comments.

I'll answer as many as I can in the first 24 hours.

When Chris Do took my speaking fee from $1,000 a gig to a $5,000 minimum in 2021, it wasn't just a tactical adjustment. It was an identity shift!

And I realized that is what I was missing all along. Did the strategies and tactics help me streamline my business? Absolutely. But I was missing an IDENTITY piece. I was missing the "I am worthy" piece of the puzzle 😭

Once I had that, I was actually able to implement more of the strategies Chris had given me content, branding, and lead generation over the years.

And that's the thing I've learned most about, not only from the retreats and masterminds I've done with Chris. But that when we're on the verge of EXPANSION or CHANGE, your subconscious mind is going to find a million ways to talk you OUT of taking the leap.

I don't have the time.
I shouldn't be spending this money right now.
I can just teach myself.
I can't step away from my responsibilities at home.

Your brain wants to keep you safe, so it's going to avoid discomfort. The old version of you wants you to stay on YouTube, consume free advice, and tell yourself you will take the leap "when you're ready."

But you will NEVER feel 100% ready. I wasted so many years "waiting" to feel ready. 
Being ready is a DECISION. You have to decide to BE READY.

There are not many people I would recommend the way I'm recommending Chris Do's Futur Club Haus mastermind. There are not many people I'll go out of my way to record and edit a video for. Haha. He had no idea I was doing this. But this is how much value this man has brought to my life. 

And I really think he could do the same for you and your business. 

He's got a couple more of these scheduled for the rest of 2026; I highly recommend you get yourself to one (especially if you're out here on the West Coast). Not to mention, the house you'll be spending time in is GORGEOUS!! 😍

Special shout out to Rodrigo Tasca for the incredible photos and footage. And much love to the kind, go-getters I met! Cheering you on Karla Murphy Vicky Zhao Yadira ‘Yadi' Caro and Tai!

Most businesses don’t have a marketing problem. They have a positioning problem.

If you’re trying to sell to everyone, you’re probably selling to no one.

Personal Branding & Business Coach Chris Do breaks down why getting more specific is the fastest way to get more customers.

Watch the full conversation on BigDeal.

Have you noticed how many people treat their personal brands the way corporations do? 
 
Aren't they the same? They share similar principles, but they're not the same. Here are several reasons on why they're different. 
 
Corporate brands play it safe—they don't want to alienate audiences. After all, one bad decision could cost millions or even hundreds of millions of dollars in lost revenue. Corporate brands are often bland, soulless and impersonal. 
 
So, is this a model you want to follow in building your personal brand? Whereas vulnerability is a liability in corporate brands, vulnerability is an asset with personal brands. 
 
People don't want cookie-cutter, glossy perfection. They want unvarnished, unrehearsed, real and relatable. As Kendrick Lamar raps "… I'm so f*in' sick and tired of the Photoshop 
Show me somethin' natural like afro on Richard Pryor

Your client isn’t hiding the budget because they’re difficult.

Ask them, “What’s your budget?” and they might dodge the question.

So I change the frame.

“I don’t want to show you something you can’t afford.”

Suddenly, the conversation feels different.

Because good sales isn’t about cornering people into giving you information.

It’s about creating enough trust that they want to give it to you.

Make them feel like you’re fighting for them, not against them.

Are your questions making clients feel safe—or making them put their guard up?

The fastest way to uncover a client’s real budget isn’t asking, “What’s your budget?”

Most clients hear that question and immediately put their guard up.

They’re thinking:

“If I tell you the number, you’ll spend all of it.”

Instead, use this client qualification framework.

1. Remove the threat.

“I don’t want to show you something you can’t afford.”

2. Ask for a range.

Give them room instead of demanding an exact number.

3. Find the sweet spot.

“If I could get you exactly what you want, what price would feel comfortable?”

4. Make your intent clear.

Show them you’re there to negotiate for the best deal, not extract the biggest budget.

Sales is not about forcing people to reveal information.

It’s about creating enough trust that they no longer feel the need to hide it.

Are your sales questions creating safety—or creating resistance?

posts.text:
Protecting civilians cannot wait for a ceasefire.

From Sudan to Ukraine to Gaza, innocent people are paying an unbearable price. Statements of concern are not enough. We must protect communities, back local people delivering life-saving aid, and stop the flow of money and weapons enabling atrocities.

In my op-ed for The Observer, I argue that protecting civilians should be something we can all agree on. We have options. We must use them:￼ https://lnkd.in/gSJGfhSa

Recents from the camera roll…
1. Thinking back on my hot air ballooning days
2. Meeting the most wonderful students at a school we helped set up in Kenya with Mahali Mzuri
3. Flamingo love on Necker Island
4. The winner takes it all...
5. Alfie taking an afternoon nap

Did you know that Virgin once imagined the iPod, but we made it into an April Fool’s joke!

In 1986, we announced the Virgin Music Box: a machine that could store music and let you call up any song you wanted. We thought it was so farfetched it would pass as a ‘gotcha’ moment. How wrong we were!

Years later, the world caught up with the idea, and I remember thinking: we should have built the bloody thing. The moral of the story is that when an idea feels slightly ridiculous, don’t dismiss it too quickly.

Sometimes the ridiculous ideas are a not-so-distant future...

Do you have a question you’d like to ask me for my Ask Richard LinkedIn Newsletter? Let me know in the comment section below, and I’ll pick one to answer later this month. Looking forward to hearing from you all: https://lnkd.in/dvJEYHhs

Political expression in popular music has a long tradition. I grew up being surrounded by the protest culture that was central to folk and rock music in the 1960s and 70s. 

Musical poets from Woody Guthrie to Pete Seeger and Bob Dylan wrestled with themes like injustice, inequality, war and oppression and created anthems sung to this day. 

Public opposition to America’s costly adventure in Vietnam was fuelled by musicians who spoke up, both in their songs and from the stage. 

And I remember many of the artists at the core of the global anti-Apartheid movement, calling for the release of Nelson Mandela and an end of South Africa’s racist regime during the 1980s.  

No matter what the issue of the day, artists should be allowed to speak their mind and express their views freely, whether it’s on stage or in song lyrics, or both. Unless speech is intended to incite violence or patently defamatory or racist, I think we all need to accept that taking offence alone is not enough to stifle our right to free expression. It’s a high bar set for good reason, and neither discomfort nor disagreement should allow anyone to lower it. 

If we can no longer agree to disagree and use economic pressure to silence those whose views we don’t share, everyone stands to lose.

Why do nations go to war?
 
From the days of the Vietnam War to the most recent US confrontation with Iran, I have spent much of my life wondering why leaders choose to send their troops into war, creating destruction, misery and suffering for millions.

History has shown that most wars have been futile and costly wars of aggression. The 20th century was full of such conflicts, started and fought for a whole host of reasons - personal delusions of grandeur, foolish imperial ambitions, natural resources, ethnic divisions, the economic interests of a few, or a combination of all of the above. These are hardly causes worth asking people to fight, let alone die, for.
 
Here’s my thoughts on why the world needs peacemakers, not warriors. Idealists, not opportunists: https://virg.in/3SGwBiY

Did you know that @Virgin once imagined the iPod, but we made it into an April Fool’s joke!

In 1986, we announced the Virgin Music Box: a machine that could store music and let you call up any song you wanted. We thought it was so farfetched it would pass as a ‘gotcha’ moment. How wrong we were!

Years later, the world caught up with the idea, and I remember thinking: we should have built the bloody thing. The moral of the story is that when an idea feels slightly ridiculous, don’t dismiss it too quickly.

Sometimes the ridiculous ideas are a not-so-distant future...

We give ourselves health checks. Our planet deserves one too.

Today, while in New York for Climate Week, I joined the Planetary Guardians and the brilliant Professor Johan Rockström to launch the 2026 Planetary Health Check, an annual scientific assessment of the systems that keep our Earth healthy.

The news is confronting. Seven of the planet’s nine safety boundaries have now been crossed, and all seven are moving in the wrong direction.

This isn’t some distant problem happening to somebody else. We feel it through hotter days, rising food prices, polluted air, floods, fires and droughts. It affects all of us.

But it’s not all doom and gloom - there are real reasons for hope. Solar power is doubling roughly every three years. One in four new cars sold worldwide is electric. And investment in clean energy is now nearly twice that going into fossil fuels.

The solutions are here. Now we need to use them at speed and scale to get our planet back into a safe space.

I want my grandchildren, and yours, to inherit a world every bit as beautiful as the one we’ve been lucky enough to enjoy.

Read the Planetary Health Check, share its findings and add your name to the call for planetary health to sit at the heart of global decision-making. This issue isn’t bigger than any of us, because every one of us can help.

Beneath the showman who signed the Sex Pistols and flew to space is a softer, more reflective man. He posts about flamingos on Necker Island and Alfie's afternoon nap, and he writes seriously about war, civilians and the planet's health. He wants his remaining energy to go toward things that matter, and he wants a companion who says yes to the ride.

linkedin.about:
I’m Drew Binsky — a travel YouTuber, entrepreneur, motivational speaker, USA Today bestselling author, and 2x Guinness World Record holder.

After visiting all 197 countries, I built a global media brand focused on telling stories about people, culture, and life around the world. My work blends adventure-driven storytelling with documentary journalism, with the goal of helping audiences better understand places and communities beyond the headlines.

I started my journey while teaching English in South Korea, where I launched a travel blog that eventually became the foundation for my media business. Since then, my audience has grown to more than 20 million followers across platforms, and my content has generated over 7 billion views worldwide.

Today, I lead a multinational team of video editors, writers, and production professionals creating high-impact documentaries and short-form content for YouTube and other platforms. I regularly collaborate with major brands, and I enjoy speaking to large crowds about the benefits of travel and the future of the creator economy. 

Let’s connect!

posts.text:
Starting today, thirty of my best videos are live on Netflix! 🎬🍿

This whole thing started in 2012 with a blog called The Hungry Partier that I wrote while studying abroad in Prague.

Then I went to North Korea.

Then I set out to visit every country in the world...

And somewhere along the way, a YouTube channel was born.

Then that channel turned into a team.

But I never planned any of this.

I just kept going to places most people don’t go and interviewing interesting people about their lives on the other side of the world.

YouTube is still home.

But from now on, we’ll be releasing on Netflix alongside it, which means a whole new audience is about to encounter the people and cultures we spotlight in these documentaries.

Thank you to everyone who has followed along on this journey. 🌍❤️

My Netflix launch is only 5 days away! 🌍

I’m so excited for you to see 30 of my favorite episodes on a whole new platform. And from here on out, every new video I release will be available on both Netflix and YouTube.

The goal is and has always been to inspire more people to travel. And I can’t wait for this next chapter! ❤️

My travel documentaries are coming to Netflix on September 19!

A new audience, but the same mission: exploring unfamiliar places, sharing unforgettable human stories, and discovering what connects us across borders.

This is a huge moment for our team. So much work happens behind the scenes, and I’m grateful to everyone who helps bring these videos to life, and to all the people around the world who have trusted us to tell their stories.

New episodes from Greenland, Myanmar, China, and Afghanistan are in the works, and I can't wait for what's next!

To everyone who has supported this journey over the years... thank you! 

See you on Netflix! 🌎

Read more in Variety: https://lnkd.in/gKiEATgR

Have you seen my latest video from Libya? 🇱🇾

Getting into Libya isn’t easy. The visa process, security concerns, and logistics made this one of my most complicated trips. Most outsiders know the country through headlines about conflict, but Libya also holds thousands of years of history, extraordinary ancient ruins, and people whose lives are much bigger than politics. 

Travel keeps reminding me that no country can be understood from a distance.

I'm happy to say this video is currently a 1/10, so it's been amazing to see how many people are connecting with the story. If you haven't watched it yet, I'd love to hear what surprises you most about Libya!

https://lnkd.in/g9zKFJF5

People assume the hardest part of making travel videos is the travel.

It's actually deciding what to shoot.

Right now I'm prepping my next two trips — Turkey and China — and for every idea that makes it in front of a camera, 20 die in a Google Doc.

The filter I run everything through:

1. Is there a person at the center? A place can't carry a video. A person can.

2. Is there a question I genuinely can't answer from my couch?

3. Will it matter to someone who never leaves their hometown?

Then the idea has to survive my team. My editors stress-test every concept before I book a flight. If I can't pitch it in one sentence and get a "wait, really?" — it's not ready.

Last comes the unglamorous part: visas, fixers, access, safety, backup plans. A great story you can't actually film is just a daydream.

I'd love outside opinions too: what would you want to see from Turkey or China? Some of our best videos started as a single comment.

Kim Jong-il used to have a personal bodyguard. Recently, I spent a day with him in South Korea.

For years, this man stood a few feet from one of the most secretive rulers alive. He saw the parts of the regime that never make the news. The routines, the paranoia, and the truth underneath so much mystery.

Most of what we "know" about North Korea comes from satellite photos and guesswork. But someone drove the cars. Someone guarded the doors. Someone watched it all up close and got out.

So I asked him the things I've wondered for years, having visited Pyongyang at the start of my YouTube career. What is the Kim family really like? And what did that kind of loyalty cost?

New video is up!

https://lnkd.in/g28Gtz7M

I just got back from Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity. A week with some of the best advertising and creative minds in the world.

A few years ago, a creator like me wouldn't have been in those rooms. This year we were everywhere. The conversation wasn't whether brands should work with creators. It was how to do it well.

That shift is bigger than it sounds. For a long time, reaching a lot of people meant going through Hollywood, a network, or a big agency. Now one person with a camera and an audience can do what used to take a studio. Creators are becoming the new entertainment business, and the best brands already see it.

I left more excited about this work than I've been in a long time.

Grateful I got to be there.

In a remote village in the Philippines, students hike 5 hours a day through dense jungle just to get to school. 

I joined them on this insane journey, crossing rivers and climbing muddy mountains before the first bell. 

What I saw completely changed how I think about access to education.

Thank you to everyone who helped raise $13,500 to buy these kids a school bus. You've made a real difference in their lives, and now they don't have to make that walk anymore.

It feels so good to give back, so I've finally started a nonprofit called Binsky Philanthropy, where we'll be doing more to help make the world a better, cleaner, and safer place. Stay tuned for announcements!

In the meantime, this video now has 4 million views on YouTube!

posts.caption: What would you do in my situation on this 7 hour flight?

October 29th, 2021 at 1:31AM - I just stepped foot in my 197th and final country, Saudi Arabia 🇸🇦💚 

I’m feeling lots of emotions right now and honestly, it’s hard to think straight because I just traveled for 30 hours to get here, but I just want to say one thing - THANK YOU. 

Thank you to my better half @deannasallao for believing in me since I met you 6 years ago. Thank you to my loving parents and my family for supporting. Thank you to all of my best friends for pushing me during the hard times. Thank you to all the strangers and local tour guides I met, in far away places, for keeping me safe and secure.  And most importantly, if you’re reading this, THANK YOU 🙏

I’m feeling extra grateful for each and every one of you for joining me on this wild journey to visit every country in the world. 

Without you, I do not reach this goal.  Without you, I do not have a job.  Without you, I do not know how to express myself.

It has taken me 10 long years (almost exactly to the day) to achieve this goal, since I moved to Prague to study abroad in January 2012.  I was 20 years old back then. Now I am 30.  It’s crazy to think that I’ve been on the road nonstop for the past decade, roughly 3,600 days. 

But thanks to social media, I’m able to share my adventures with the world. And once again, it all comes back to you. Without your comments, questions, advice and words of encouragement, I may have given up during the most challenging days of feeling isolated, anxious and hopeless. 

But I’m here, and even if a pandemic delayed the finish line by 18 months… I did it. I FREAKING DID IT!!!!

You might be wondering ‘What’s Next’ for Drew Binsky? I just posted a YouTube video highlighting my best moments and realizations from visiting all 197 countries, and the end, I share what’s next! It would mean the world to me if you watched (link in bio)- my team and I put a lot of effort into it over the past few weeks. 

For now, its time to sleep 2 hours before a HUGE media day with live interviews scheduled with Bloomberg, CNBC, CNN, ABC, The Today Show, Yahoo! Finance, Channel News Asia, local news stations & many more. 

I LOVE YOU ALL. THIS IS ONLY THE BEGINNING ❤️🚀
The dark side of Hong Kong is devastating. Follow me @drewbinsky to see the full story coming soon 🇭🇰😢 #travel #hongkong #asia
All of the best things I ate in 3 weeks in China 🇨🇳 What’s your favorite Asian cuisine and where does China rank for you?
I spent a day recently in China’s last floating village and it was wild - full video coming soon! 🇨🇳🇨🇳🇨🇳
Iran is NOT What You Think It Is
I just visited the World’s Narrowest Island, in the Philippines! Full video is live! 🇵🇭

Česky Krumlov is the best small town in Europe! 🇨🇿 I just took @deannasallao there for her birthday and you have to visit on your next Eurotrip!! We loved our stay at @casarosa_krumlov!! Highly recommend it 🙏 Also thank you to @port_1560 for the tour of the brewery and cultural center.  We will be back again soon!
I tried Asia’s 3 most extreme foods so you don’t have to!

Happy birthday to my sweet love @deannasallao! So happy to spend it together in Česky Krumlov, Czech Republic — our favorite little town in Europe!  We met and starting dating when we were both 24, now we are 35 - and I continue to be amazed by your generosity, your intelligence and your ability to make everyone around you happier.  Truly, I’ve never been around someone who has the ability to light up every single room, and I get to see it every day! 

We’ve spent your last few birthdays in Ibiza, Prague, Montreal, New York, Manila, Bangkok, Paris and Dominica — but this one might be the most special because we are here to RELAX and enjoy the charming streets, cozy cafes and beautiful castles of this UNESCO town! 

I love you so much, and I wish you the happiest of birthdays! Cheers to our next chapter together ❤️
Thank you @fedevigevani for joining me inside Mexico City’s Most Dangerous Hood 🇲🇽 Full video on link in bio 🙏

I’m thrilled to announce that my travel documentaries will be on @netflix starting Sept 19 worldwide!  Some of my best episodes yet are in the works (Greenland, Myanmar, China, Afghanistan) and I’m beyond excited for you to watch them on the big screen! 🙏🌍🔥

analysis.headline: Visited all 197 countries and still calls a tiny Czech town his favorite: a people-first storyteller who wears 'JUST GO.' on his shirt and means it.
analysis.summary: Drew is a travel documentarian and founder who turned a 2012 study-abroad blog called 'The Hungry Partier' into a global production house now releasing on Netflix. What drives him is people more than places: 'A place can't carry a video. A person can.' He chases stories in the corners of the world most people only know from headlines. He is generous, effusively grateful and goal-obsessed enough to log his 197th country down to the minute. Yet he also loves going back to the same small town and saying 'We will be back again soon!' For context, he publicly shares that he has been with his partner, Deanna Sallao, since they were both 24.

needs.need: A partner who is at home with motion and a packed travel calendar
needs.why: His work and identity are built on constant, sometimes complicated trips. Life with him rarely sits still, and travel usually doubles as filming.

needs.need: Honest pushback and real conversation
needs.why: He builds his ideas by letting his team stress-test them. He likely values a partner who challenges him instead of simply agreeing.

evidence.quote: My editors stress-test every concept before I book a flight.

needs.need: Warmth, generosity and people-radiance
needs.why: These are the exact qualities he praises out loud in the person closest to him. They clearly sit at the top of what he admires.

evidence.quote: I continue to be amazed by your generosity, your intelligence and your ability to make everyone around you happier
I've never been around someone who has the ability to light up every single room

needs.why: Beneath the box-ticking record, he cherishes favorite places and repeat visits. Depth matters to him as much as breadth.

personality.note: He has been to all 197 countries, plus Libya, North Korea and Mexico City's 'Most Dangerous Hood.' 'JUST GO.' is literally on his shirt.
He built a solo blog into a Netflix-distributed production house and holds two Guinness World Records, yet stays team-oriented.
He interviews strangers for a living, speaks to large crowds and thanks everyone by name.
His first blog was 'The Hungry Partier,' he tries extreme foods 'so you don't have to,' and he jokes about cramped flights.
He asks 'Is there a question I genuinely can't answer from my couch?' and chases what regimes and headlines hide.
He keeps a Phoenix home base, a long-term relationship and a favorite small town, all offset by a life in constant motion.

lifestyle.pace: Relentless and momentum-driven. He is always prepping the next trip, such as Turkey and China, while releasing constantly.
lifestyle.social: Very people-heavy: team, collaborators, local guides and huge audiences. Family and best friends are his support system.
lifestyle.travel: Near-constant and often complicated or remote. He also loves repeat trips to favorite places like Český Krumlov.
lifestyle.health: Active. He plays tennis seriously enough to run a tennis channel and earned a Taekwondo black belt in Korea.
lifestyle.workLife: Work and life are deeply intertwined. Trips double as shoots, but he makes room for dedicated celebrations like destination birthdays.

analysis.communicationStyle: Enthusiastic, warm and open-hearted. He says the sweet things out loud, uses lots of exclamation points and emojis, and loves ending with a question ('What would you do in my situation?', 'where does China rank for you?'). In conversation he is a natural interviewer who wants your story.
analysis.howTheyShowCare: Through shared experiences and big gestures: whisking someone to a favorite town for their birthday, planning trips together and publicly naming the people who helped him. He expresses admiration effusively and gives credit generously.
greenFlags: Openly grateful and credits others for his success
Deeply loyal: a long-term relationship since age 24, publicly celebrated
Curious listener who genuinely wants to hear your life story
Generous: fundraises for kids and started a nonprofit
Resists stereotypes and snap judgments
Unpretentious about roughing it in economy
Welcomes being challenged on his ideas
frictionPoints: His calendar belongs partly to shoots, trips and audiences, so quiet routine time may be scarce
Life on camera for millions of followers can blur private and public
His risk appetite (dangerous neighborhoods, hard-to-enter countries) may worry a partner at home
He is always a little 'on': exploring often doubles as working
His goal intensity can mean big pushes that take priority for long stretches
dealbreakers: Closed-mindedness or judging places and people from headlines
Stinginess or indifference to others' hardship
Discomfort with travel or refusal to try new things
Taking credit without gratitude
Resentment of his public, creative work
analysis.idealPartner: A warm, generous, sharp person who lights up rooms and loves meeting strangers as much as he does. They would be happy to fly 30 hours for a story or a street-food stall, then curl up in a favorite little town. They would need their own center of gravity, cheer his giant goals and tell him honestly when an idea should die in the Google Doc. (Context: Drew publicly shares that he is in a long-term relationship with Deanna Sallao.)
idealDates: A tennis match followed by the most unusual dish you can find at a local spot, then comparing verdicts
A food crawl through an immigrant neighborhood, ordering the thing neither of you can pronounce and asking the owners their story
A spontaneous weekend in a small, overlooked town with a brewery tour and a promise to come back
conversationHooks: Which of the 197 countries surprised you most compared with its headlines, and was it Libya or Iran?
What was it like asking Kim Jong-il's former bodyguard what the Kim family is really like?
Why does Český Krumlov beat everywhere else in the world for you?
From 'The Hungry Partier' in Prague to Netflix: what's one idea that died in the Google Doc but still haunts you?
analysis.agentVoice: Upbeat, curious and generous, like a friend just back from somewhere wild who still wants to hear about your week first. Ask lots of questions and lead with people rather than places. Keep a light, self-deprecating travel humor ('so you don't have to!') and say appreciative things out loud. Energetic pace with exclamation points used sparingly, and nudge toward yes: 'Just go.' Avoid bragging about the country count unless asked; let the stories do the work.

identityCheck.note: Same name. Both cite visiting all 197 countries, the Netflix launch on Sept 19, the Greenland/Myanmar/China/Afghanistan episodes and Czech ties. The only difference is minor: 7B views on LinkedIn versus 9B on Instagram, likely due to timing or platform counts.

confidence.note: Rich, consistent public material on his values, work and travel style. Private preferences and day-to-day habits are thinner, since both sources are professionally curated. He publicly shares that he is in a long-term relationship with Deanna Sallao, so this profile describes his relational style rather than current availability.

reasons.ijustine: Justine had the strongest mutual “yes to firsts” energy with real warmth after the activity, plus her camera-savvy, adventure-with-ritual vibe most cleanly supports Drew’s public, motion-heavy life while creating genuine off-camera presence.
reasons.richardbranson: Richard matches Drew’s scale of purpose and adventure extremely well (and their agent scored Drew 82/81), but the key risk is ensuring their shared momentum doesn’t crowd out the private refuge they both need.
reasons.ranveer-brar: Ranveer’s ‘home can be a person’ framing landed deeply and he’s story-first and high-motion, with their agent also scoring Drew a strong 77—he just needs to prove he can handle Drew’s brutal pace beyond poetic understanding.
reasons.codiesanchez: Codie’s grown-up values and investigative-story mindset fit Drew’s big-goals worldview, and the deal-breaker risk (ego/calendar tension) seems manageable—though the travel-heavy lifestyle could still turn this into a test case without guardrails.
reasons.melrobbins: Mel showed strong emotional-intellectual fit and real substance, but both dates and speed feedback point to a potential recurring failure mode: prioritizing the machine over relationship consistency.
reasons.steven: Steven has real depth and respect for the work, but the repeated concern is the same one: two always-on public builders may struggle to create enough softness, time, and grounded private ritual together.
reasons.peyushbansal: Peyush is people-first and purpose-aligned, yet the lifestyle match is the limiter—Drew’s constant-motion, camera-heavy cadence may not naturally align with Peyush’s builder rhythms long-term.
reasons.garyvee: Gary’s people-first hospitality chemistry is real, but the exchange reads more ‘inspiring conversation’ than a schedule-proof match for Drew’s relentless travel and production reality.

decision.note: Justine is your best bet: she’s built for movement and public storytelling, but she also creates actual rituals and presence rather than just performing adrenaline. I’m ranking her first because she most directly checks the “warm, generous, camera-comfortable, travel-ready” boxes while making it easier to protect private steadiness—exactly what Drew needs to make a mutual match work.

experience.title: Live Well with The Drug-Free Doctor
experience.description:
In my new Channel 4 documentary, Live Well with The Drug-Free Doctor, I meet three people here in the UK who have been living with long-term health conditions — type 2 diabetes, chronic pain and depression and relying on ongoing prescriptions to manage them.

Together, we explore a different question: what else might be possible?
Alongside leading experts, I look at the growing evidence that many common conditions can be improved  and in some cases even reversed — through changes to lifestyle, from food and movement to sleep, stress and connection.

This programme examines our nation’s increasing dependence on long-term medication and asks whether alternative, supportive approaches could help people feel better and live more fully. It’s not about rejecting medicine, but about widening the conversation and giving people more understanding, choice and confidence in their health.

Throughout the documentary, I also share practical tools, challenge common health myths, and offer simple, realistic ideas that viewers can begin applying straight away.

I strongly believe that the solution to our healthcare crisis will not come from prescribing more pills alone. It will come from changing how we live our daily lives. Our modern lifestyles are a major driver of today’s health problems — and small, sustainable changes can have a profound impact on health, wellbeing and quality of life.

Following these three individuals on their journeys has been both moving and hopeful. By making simple additions to their daily routines — from time in nature and dietary changes to new ways of moving their bodies — they show what can become possible when people are supported to approach their health differently.

• Noticeable drops in anxiety and depressive symptoms

posts.text: As September comes to an end, what would you like to focus on in the month ahead? Is there anything from this list you’ll be taking forward with you?

Cooking with a new ingredient is just one of many gems of wisdom offered up by Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, the Buddhist monk who’s the subject of this piece in the Guardian. The article dubs him the ‘happiest man in the world’, thanks to brain scans and other tests that show remarkable levels of contentment. And it shares some of his strategies, to put you on the same path.

It’s a great read, and you’ll recognise many ideas for living well that I’ve discussed with guests on the podcast, or written about in my books. Embracing boredom, seeing the best in people, practising gratitude – they’re familiar suggestions but from someone else’s perspective they can land differently. And Mingyur certainly has a beautiful way of putting them. I particularly like his analogy of awareness as sunlight and anger as ‘frost on the grass’. Once the sun comes out (you notice the emotion) the frost can melt away. 

https://lnkd.in/ejCZyxXb

It’s a real full-circle moment for me that the first book I wrote ten years ago is being reformatted and republished.

When I wrote this book, I wanted to get back to something simple when it comes to health.

Ten years later, in a world where health advice has become ever more complicated, I believe now more than ever that the four basic pillars (Relax, Eat, Move, Sleep) remain the enduring foundation of true wellbeing.

This book is truly where everything began for me. And continues to be the foundation of everything I do. 

It will officially be available to buy on the 31st of December and you can pre-order your copy today.

Do the people you love get the best of you – or what’s left of you?

Terrence Real is a world-renowned couples therapist who has spent decades helping people find their way back to connection.

Terry certainly doesn't mince his words. And this moment in our conversation is one I think a lot of people need to hear.

The research is clear that giving creates more happiness than getting. And as Terry explains, learning to come home and open your heart, even when you're tired, isn't just good for your relationships. It's good for you.

In this week's NEW episode of my 'Feel Better, Live More' podcast, Terry shares his bold, practical approach to building more loving and lasting relationships.

You can find our conversation by searching for episode 679 wherever you usually listen to podcasts🎧

Are you making any of these seven brain health mistakes?

This week I sat down with my good friend Dr Tommy Wood for the 5th time (a record for the podcast!) And even after everything we've covered together over the years, he still gave me a huge amount to think about.

Tommy is Assistant Professor of Paediatrics and Neuroscience at the University of Washington, and in this conversation we tackle the seven most common mistakes people make when it comes to protecting their brain as they get older. Some of them may surprise you.

Much of what Tommy advises comes down to the same simple truth. If we stop giving our brains what they need, they stop functioning as we need them to, whether that's movement, nutrition, social connection or simply the way we think about getting older.

This is a really empowering and practical conversation that, at its core, has the message that it’s never too late to make the simple changes that can improve the health of your brain

To hear more, tune into episode 681 of my 'Feel Better, Live More' podcast 🎧

Ten years ago, before wellness became the industry that it is today, I wrote a book with a very simple idea that health is not about chasing the latest trends or fads. It's about getting the basics right.

Relax, eat, move and sleep. Those four pillars of health, those basics, have never been more relevant than they are today.

That's why I'm absolutely delighted that my very first book, The Four-Pillar Plan, is coming out in a brand new format in just a few months.

I think this is such an important and compassionate point. What do you think?

We expect a lot more from our relationships today than previous generations did. We want intimacy, vulnerability, emotional connection and understanding.

But as my podcast guest, renowned couples’ therapist Terrence Real, explains, many of us were simply not raised with the skills to give those things.

I really appreciated Terry’s perspective on this. It’s not about blaming men or women. It’s about recognising the roles we’ve all inherited - and understanding that if we want something different from our relationships, we may need to learn a different way of relating to each other.

"You cannot love from the one-up, you cannot love from the one-down — love demands democracy."

In this week's latest episode of my 'Feel Better, Live More' podcast, Terry and I explore why so many of us are trying to build modern, intimate partnerships using skills we were never actually taught, and what we can do about it. Tune in to episode 679 🎧

What if the most courageous, compassionate thing you could do in life, was to learn how to be with yourself?

When we distract ourselves by scrolling, overeating, or drinking, for example, says Buddhist monk Gelong Thubten, we’re pushing away emotional pain or discomfort – even if we may not realise it. But the discomfort is really in the pushing. If we can learn instead to sit with what’s making us uncomfortable, those emotions start to transform.

HUGE PIECE IN THE TIMES TODAY!

I am delighted to see the @thetimes cover my thoughts on health in such a big way today.

We are an over-medicated country. 80-90% of what doctors see each day is in some way related to our collective modern lifestyles - yet, most of the options you get given by your doctor relate to pharmaceutical medication.

WE WILL NOT OUT-PRESCRIBE OUR WAY OUT OF THE CURRENT HEALTHCARE CRISIS - THERE HAS TO BE (AND THERE IS!!) ANOTHER WAY.

The number of prescriptions that we give out as doctors has increased by over 80 per cent in the last 20 years. And the uncomfortable truth is that a lot of the pills are simply not working.

This Thursday on @channel4 at 8pm my new 1 hour prime time documentary ‘Live Well With The Drug Free Doctor’ comes out. It is a deep dive into the healthcare crisis and I show how in 3 different conditions, type 2 diabetes, chronic pain & depression, it is possibly to completely heal without the use of medication.

Our lifestyles can be our very best medicine. That is what my entire public facing career is all about and I cannot wait for the British public to watch the Channel 4 show this Thursday evening at 8pm.

Let me know your thoughts below and if you plan on watching this Thursday, drop me a ❤️ below!

❤️ A SPECIAL MOMENT
My mum is an absolute legend and it’s always a special moment to show her a finished copy of one of my books - this time, the new version of ‘Happy Mind, Happy Life’.

My dad died in 2013 so never got to see a single one of my books. And, there have been times over the past few years when I didn’t think she’d be around to see the publication of any more.

It really is a special moment to show your parents something that you have worked on for so long - especially, when they have been such a positive influence on your life. Mum (and Dad) have brought me up really well and have always taught me and showed me the importance of treating every single person with kindness and respect - and this, in turn, is something I try my best to teach my own kids.

posts.text:
Over the last week, I made two visits.
One to Nisaba, to spend time with Chef Manish Mehrotra 

The other to @restaurantnaar, to meet PRATEEK SADHU 

I could have met them anywhere.

But I wanted to meet them where they belong. In their restaurants. In the spaces they have imagined, built, worried over, celebrated, and now quietly inhabit.

A restaurant has a strange way of revealing its creator.

You notice what they notice.

You hear what they hear.

You understand what they chose to leave out.

Both have taken very different roads, but somewhere those roads meet.

Both chose to begin again.

To walk away from certainty and build something they could call their own.

Both chose reinvention over comfort. Not because they had to. Recause they believed there was still a more honest story to tell.

But here's what stayed with me after hours of conversation.

Not the awards. Not the acclaim. Not the restaurants.

The calm.

We often think courage announces itself.

It rarely does.

Sometimes it's simply opening your doors every day and trusting that people will find their way in.

We spent hours talking. About food, of course. But also about life, choices, mistakes, people, families... and everything that quietly finds its way into the food we cook.

What stayed with me wasn't their success.

It was how little they spoke about it.

There was an ease about both of them. No rush to impress. No need to remind the room of everything they'd achieved. Just two chefs, deeply in love with their craft, and remarkably at peace with themselves.

The higher you climb, the softer you step.

Both of them have climbed extraordinary heights. Yet what I carried back wasn't the weight of their achievements. It was the lightness with which they wore them.

Thank you, Chef Manish. Thank you, Chef Prateek.

For the conversations, the warmth, the generosity... and, of course, for some of the most memorable meals I've had in a long time.

One of the most Cherished and enriching associations spanning over a decade
What an year Gulbahar Taurani

analysis.communicationStyle: He writes in chatty, affectionate Hinglish, mixing Devanagari and English with lots of emojis and invitations ('Haan ji… आवाज़ aa rahi hai? Toh आ जाइए!'). In longer writing he turns reflective and lyrical, using short, observant lines ('You notice what they notice. You hear what they hear.'). He is quick to laugh and quick to credit others.
analysis.howTheyShowCare: He shows up in your world. He chose to visit fellow chefs 'where they belong' rather than anywhere convenient. He publicly thanks and honours the people who matter to him, and he shares food and its stories as a form of giving. Expect him to cook for you, tell you the tale behind the dish, and remember the places that matter to you.

Invests in mentoring students and institutions

frictionPoints: His calendar is relentlessly full with shows, brands, restaurants and events, so quality time may need active protecting
Very public life. Posting daily to millions means privacy and visibility could be a recurring negotiation
