lifestyle.workLife: Deliberately blurred: she hosts a retailer's 100th birthday on her basketball team's home court, calls the collision of work, fashion and sport "thriving", and brings the same people into both worlds.

analysis.communicationStyle: Fast, funny and blunt, with the punchline usually doing the arguing for her. She mixes earnest long-form advocacy with one-liners — "Let's get to work", "Get out of office, you don't know how to lead. - Ms. Singh" — and signs her opinions with her own name as if daring you to disagree. Emojis, em-dashes and direct address are her punctuation; she says the thing rather than hinting at it.
analysis.howTheyShowCare: By hyping you publicly and loudly. She made 'Chief Hype Officer' an actual title, credited with 'keeping the energy HYPE', and she celebrates other people's wins in her own feed — Anthem Awards "Go team 👏🏽", "Proud to be part of this team." She also protects: "fiercely protective of its players." Expect encouragement, amplification and a willingness to fight on your behalf.
greenFlags: Puts her own money behind her stated values instead of just posting about them
Celebrates teammates and collaborators in public and by name
Self-deprecating and quick to laugh at herself
Reflects annually and publicly on what her work actually achieved
Says hard things plainly rather than letting them fester
Direct about boundaries, rest and self-worth — including her own struggle to hold them
Gracious with press and collaborators: "Thank you ELLE Magazine India for a lovely time and great write up!"
frictionPoints: The pace is relentless — a partner who wants slow, spontaneous, unscheduled togetherness will often come second to a launch, a shoot or a game.
Her public platform means parts of the relationship will be visible or speculated about; she is not going to hide her life.
She is blunt and her opinions are signed. Arguments are likely to be direct and quick rather than delicate.
Her advocacy is non-negotiable, so a partner who prefers to stay apolitical or neutral on gender issues will feel friction here.
The 'Daddy' caretaker framing in her bio suggests she defaults to looking after people — which can crowd out being looked after.
She admits the boundary-setting is still a work in progress, so she may overgive before she asks for what she needs.
dealbreakers: Transphobia — "Sit ALL the way down with your transphobia and tomfoolery."
Anyone using women's safety as a costume for clout
People who position themselves as experts on her field without the track record — "Get out of office, you don't know how to lead."
Passivity: someone with no drive of their own to be hyped about
Needing to be the only ambitious person in the room
Expecting a partner to self-sacrifice as a demonstration of love
analysis.idealPartner: Someone with their own thriving thing going on — a builder, creator, athlete or operator who has a mission they'd say "let's get to work" about — and who is happy to be loud about hers too. They need to be unshockable, direct in return, genuinely aligned on gender equity rather than politely silent, and secure enough to share a very bright spotlight without shrinking. Bonus if they'll dance on the sidelines with her and then disappear to a quiet resort and do absolutely nothing.
idealDates: Courtside at a Toronto Tempo game, then staying for the Rhythm Section and dancing on the sidelines with her instead of leaving at the final whistle.
A museum or gallery opening night where she gets to dress up properly — a custom fit, a real outfit, and a late dinner dissecting the show afterwards.
A no-agenda resort day in the sun somewhere like the Zadun stay she posted — a drink with a straw, no phones, and a deliberate reset after a brutal stretch.
A long dinner conversation in the spirit of her unlearning episode: what you were each taught a 'good woman' or 'good man' looks like, and which parts you're both throwing out.
conversationHooks: Ask about the seven-year wait behind the film DOIN' IT — what changed in her as a first-time lead, writer and producer over those years.
Ask what HYPHEN8 is actually for and who she wants it to reach — she signs off with "Let's get to work", so ask what work.
Ask what a Chief Hype Officer really does day to day, and whether the job has taught her anything about hyping herself.
Ask where the "I don't buy Birkins, I buy sports teams" decision came from — it's clearly a values statement, not a flex.
Ask what she's still unlearning from the "we call it strength" conversation about self-sacrifice and self-worth — and whether she's actually setting boundaries yet.
Ask about holding "ten toes down" when your own league is the fight — what it costs to be the owner who speaks.
analysis.agentVoice: Sound like a co-founder who has your back and a comic who can't help the punchline. Short, declarative sentences. Warmth delivered with a bit of teasing, never gushing. Lead with her accomplishments as facts, not adjectives — "she owns two pro sports teams and her first feature is in cinemas." Use her own phrasing where it lands: "Let's get to work", "I don't buy Birkins, I buy sports teams." Be straight about the pace and the visibility up front — no softening, no overpromising. Never position her as needing to be rescued, and never let a match assume they'd be tagging along on her life rather than building their own. If someone wastes her time, a cool "Get out of office" energy is in character. Sign off with momentum, not goodbye.

identityCheck.note: Strong match: both profiles are Lilly Singh with the same headline credits (Emmy-winning actress, NYT best-selling author, Unicorn Island, HYPHEN8, Toronto Tempo part-owner/Chief Hype Officer) and the same Toronto-anchored story.

confidence.note: Rich, consistent material across both sources — career, missions, humour and lifestyle all show up repeatedly and corroborate each other. Lower certainty on day-to-day habits, downtime and private relationship patterns, which are largely inferred from a curated public feed.

reasons.emmagrede: Emma had the cleanest values + boundary-language alignment on the date, with “who holds you” translating into a shared system rather than a vibe, and only a remaining risk around schedule/public-life logistics.
reasons.garyvee: Gary and Lilly both bring direct builder energy and decent sports/rest boundary overlap, but the long-term question is whether his “rest boundaries” reliably hold when his constant motion ramps—and whether gender-equity convictions go beyond fandom.
reasons.jetslacked: Kanika showed operator-brain directness and negotiated reboot/anchor boundaries, and Lilly can genuinely benefit from her solo oxygen—but the day-to-day match-energy may thin out if solo-check-ins replace consistent encouragement and hype.
reasons.melrobbins: Mel delivered a surprisingly clean second-date-worthy values/boundary fit, with a real understanding of rest, but we still need proof she can consistently hold the line against Lilly’s relentlessly multiplying spotlight and pace.
reasons.sarablakely: Sara’s women-first mission, humor, and boundary logic fit Lilly’s values request well, but the main concern is sustainability: Lilly’s nonstop public volume may eventually feel like Sara can’t fully “stay in the room.”
reasons.financewithsharan: Sharan is a calm mission-builder with real systems credibility, but the conversations didn’t demonstrate the kind of values-vocal, gender-equity “line in the sand” alignment and hype-reciprocity Lilly actively runs on.
reasons.thespacegal: Emily brings strong warmth and women-empowerment alignment, but she reads less built for Lilly’s relentless, public, debate-forward lifestyle—so the relationship risks becoming admiration-from-afar rather than equal-part hype and direct alignment.
reasons.richardbranson: Richard’s values and big-impact storytelling fit, but the evidence points to mismatch on Lilly’s day-to-day operational pace and on meeting her competence-first, direct engagement style once the adrenaline and travel novelty fade.

decision.note: My pick is Emma Grede. The date showed the rarest thing Lilly needs: mutual, explicit boundary language tied to values (not just charisma), plus real warmth that doesn’t slide into overgiving—my only remaining worry is whether the LA↔Toronto/public-life collision stays managed without Emma defaulting to “hosting/optimizing” instead of shared leadership.

She's warm, culturally rooted and bilingual, and she'd rather laugh through an awkward conversation than sit in it.

personality.note: Says yes to collaborations and out-of-house experiences she finds exciting, but the anchor of her life is a local, repetitive practice — home gym, home city, home crew.
Six years in fast media, a 720k+ following, over 2,000 posts and branded campaigns. She builds at volume, though she frames it with jokes rather than manifestos.
A gym community she's happy to film and dance with, festival crews, collaborations, a public-facing job. Big-room energy, likely with a small inner circle.
This is the core. POV captions, mock breaking-news desks, deadlift show-off jokes, silly overlays about distracting someone from wanting an iPad.
An English honours degree, a journalism diploma, magazine writing on science, environment and health, and reading and research among her listed skills — curious but filtered through creative output.
Disciplined and deadline-tested, comfortable with routine — but she processes big life questions through deflection and jokes, which is charm and armour at once.

lifestyle.pace: Fast and full. A near-daily content cadence plus training, festivals and brand shoots — the calendar probably looks busy even when the captions are chaotic.
lifestyle.social: Big and warm. A gym crew, family jokes about her niece, festival crowds, collaborators. She's comfortable being the loudest, funniest person in the room.
lifestyle.travel: Limited evidence — outings and event visits within her orbit are documented, including an Apple showcase she called worth leaving the house for. No travel pattern to report.
lifestyle.health: Consistent gym training with clear benchmarks — deadlifts, core control, fitness as a genuine practice rather than a photo op.
lifestyle.workLife: Blended, not separated. Gym, festival and family moments all get filmed and posted; creating is woven through the day rather than confined to office hours.

analysis.communicationStyle: Rapid-fire Hinglish, heavy on POV captions, rhetorical bits and self-deprecation. She opens with a joke and keeps the tone light even when the topic is serious — periods, marriage, disappointment — using humour as the safe container. Direct underneath the silliness, and entirely comfortable being public about it.
analysis.howTheyShowCare: Playfully. She recruits herself as your big brother for Rakshabandhan rather than making a speech, turns a festival into a shared workout, teases and cheers and shows up. Practical help, funny framing, little ceremony.
greenFlags: Self-deprecating rather than self-serious — "I'm a professional idiot on the internet"
Backs a long list of causes publicly on her professional profile
Disciplined where it counts: sustained posting and a trained, goal-based gym habit
Bilingual and culturally flexible — moves between English and Hindi naturally
Comfortable discussing everyday, awkward realities instead of avoiding them
Loyal to collaborators and crews, not just to her own output
frictionPoints: Her work is a constant stream — 2,000+ posts means the phone and the edit will sometimes be the third person in the relationship
She handles 'big life topics' with jokes ('Asking my niece if I should marry'), so getting a straight answer about feelings may take patience
Her social and festival calendar runs hot; a quieter partner could feel pulled along or left out
A public-facing life means a lot of what you two do could end up on camera, which suits some and not others
Bollywood and gym humour are her registers — she may coast past a heavy moment without noticing if it doesn't land as a bit
dealbreakers: Someone who can't be laughed at, or who takes themselves too seriously to join a bit
Anyone who dismisses content creation as not a real job or not real work
Someone who is indifferent to the social causes she publicly attaches herself to
A partner who wants to keep feelings and everyday realities off the table
Someone who won't show up to the plans, the festivals or the training — she says yes, she'll want a yes back
analysis.idealPartner: Someone emotionally playful and quick — can hold a bit, can be teased, can tease back — and secure enough not to compete with a partner whose work is also her public voice. They'd have their own discipline (a gym habit, a craft, a goal), their own friends, and a real appetite for Mumbai life: festivals, shows, and being out in the city. Rooted, warm, and unbothered by the occasional camera.
idealDates: A Ganpati pandal crawl that starts silly and ends with the best street food she can find — she already turns Visarjan into a workout, so keep it moving.
A lift session at her gym followed by coffee, where the challenge is an honest attempt at her 50kg deadlift or an equivalent benchmark of yours.
A comedy open mic or theatre night, followed by a debate over what worked — she studied theatre and listing Debate as a school activity suggests she'll have opinions.
An Apple store or product-launch day out, leaning into the fact that a showcase genuinely did make her lose her mind.
conversationHooks: Ask her to explain what "Zubaan ke alawa poori body pe behtraen control pa liya hai" actually meant to her — training as control, not just results.
Ask how the Whisper 'Period Pe Charcha' series got pitched, and how she makes a taboo topic funny without making it flippant.
Ask about Miranda House theatre — what she performed, and whether she still misses a live audience.
Ask what the BuzzFeed India Bollywood desk was actually like in 2015–2018, and what she learned before she went solo.
Ask about the 'professional idiot' persona — whether the goofiness is the whole personality or partly a shield for the serious stuff.
Ask what she'd cover if she could make a 'Cognizance'-style science and environment magazine again today.
analysis.agentVoice: Bright, fast, Hinglish-adjacent and never precious. Lead with a line that makes them smile, keep the pace of a well-edited reel, and be honest about the real stuff without ever getting heavy about it. Use light POV framing when describing her ('POV: you're dating someone whose gym is also her friend group'). No ad-speak, no overselling, no listing achievements like a CV — drop one specific detail and let it do the work. Warm, self-aware, quick to laugh at ourselves.

identityCheck.note: Strong match. Her LinkedIn About explicitly names the Instagram handle she posts under ("You can find my work on Instagram @srishtipatch"), the Instagram bio name and handle match Srishti Dixit, both list Mumbai, and both describe the same job — content creation with a comedy and fitness bent. LinkedIn's celebrity/Bollywood career is consistent with Instagram's pop-culture, festival and lifestyle content.

confidence.note: Both sources are detailed and consistent, giving solid coverage of work, humour, fitness, values and cultural context. Lower confidence on romance history, travel habits and day-to-day relationship behaviour — those aren't visible in either source, and some of the funniest posts (the marriage joke, the Rakshabandhan bit) reveal tone rather than facts.

reasons.sumukhisuresh: Highest likelihood of matching Srishti’s “laugh first + discipline + values” combo, with clear evidence they can keep the gym/iteration playful without dismissing the work.
reasons.dollysingh: Strong creative/comedic wavelength and solid discipline signals, with the main risk being whether Delhi-vs-Mumbai logistics can support Srishti’s “yes means yes” festival/training cadence.
reasons.financewithsharan: Good values and compatible systems + banter energy, and likely to respect her public-facing creator reality—open question is whether he consistently joins the messy Mumbai life instead of staying in controlled recharge mode.
reasons.vineetasng: Fast chemistry on fitness/craft and clear banter potential, but Srishti needs proof they’ll reliably match her high-cadence “creating is work + go out and show up” lifestyle long-term.
reasons.drjulie: Values alignment and a playful mind for small-step discipline are strong, but distance/cadence and the risk of staying too “small-step” could delay the deeper everyday-emotional intimacy Srishti will want.
reasons.aliabdaal: A good mindset match (playful systems, values, discipline), yet the public-life/tempo mismatch raises concerns about how much of Srishti’s Mumbai visibility and social rhythm stays shared.
reasons.masabagupta: Nourishing creative energy with real values overlap, but motherhood/intensity plus both being major public creators makes attention/time tradeoffs harder to get right.
reasons.your-richbff: Super fun and smart with gym-comedy compatibility, but Miami-vs-Mumbai makes the “frequent in-person plans/festivals” requirement unlikely.

decision.note: Srishti, my pick is Sumukhi Suresh. They’ve got the strongest mix of “laugh first,” real discipline, and values alignment, and the way their comedy-process works seems compatible with Srishti’s creator-life (not just admiration for it). The only watch-out is making sure they can shift from fast-roast mode into consistent emotional presence.

posts.text:
Dear Investor,

Data helps us make better decisions. But it can also shorten our time horizon.

Think about the things we hold patiently: FDs, single malts, private businesses, even ancestral furniture in our homes. None of them come with a live NAV flashing on our phones every second.

Stocks and mutual funds are different. We can check them anytime. And because we can, we do.

Here's the irony: volatility rises the more often you look. The investment hasn't changed. Only the frequency of observation has.

Maybe the answer is to evaluate investments over the horizon they were designed for. An overnight fund can be judged daily. An equity fund probably can't.

On a lighter but no so light note, imagine if your house had a live NAV. It wouldn't become more volatile. You'd just notice the volatility more. Then you'd check it ten times a day, compare it with your neighbour's, obsess over whether you paid the right price, and have the occasional anxiety attack.

The house wouldn't have changed.

Only your experience of owning it would.

Love,

Zindagi
Thank you 🙏

This is a must watch clip of a superstar, at his absolute lowest.

There is a lesson in maintaining composure and dignity in your conduct.

There is a reminder that when everything fails, go back to your core - in his case acting.

And there is a nudge that nobody is too big to ask for an opportunity.

Most investors start with an absolute goal.

"I need 12% returns."
"I need to retire comfortably."
"I need my money to beat inflation and grow."

Then something strange happens.

The fund delivers what it promised. The goal is on track.

But a newer, hotter fund appears. It made more. Suddenly, what was good enough isn't good enough anymore.

Absolute becomes relative.

Money moves. Fund managers feel pressure to keep up. Risks get stretched. Portfolios become more aggressive. Everyone chases the latest winner.

The irony is that the investor's goal may not have changed at all.

In investing, performance matters.  Too little performance is a problem. But too much performance should also make you ask questions.

Because in markets, there is rarely a free lunch. Extraordinary returns often come with extraordinary risks, sometimes visible, sometimes hidden.

The best investing is not about finding the fund that wins every year.

It's about finding an approach that gets you where you need to go, and having the discipline to stay with it.

The biggest wealth destroyer is often not poor performance.

It's the constant search for better performance.

Many people ask me, "Do I need a SIF?"

That's the wrong question.

Don't ask for the product. Show me the problem.

- Need a more efficient alternative to traditional fixed income? Meet Hybrid Long Short (better yield solution)
- Looking for high-alpha opportunities? Meet Ex Top 100 (alpha solution)
- Want core equity exposure with a little extra alpha and lower noise? Meet Equity Long Short (efficient beta solution)

Portfolios don't need more products.  They need better solutions to existing problems.
Here is the detailed presentation of Altiva's next offering, the predictable large cap alpha solution, using income strategies.

What's one thing you need to run a company?

Resilience.

Twenty-two years in capital markets have taught me that neither success nor failure is permanent, although both can feel pretty dramatic in the moment.

Industries go in and out of favor. Technology changes. Global circumstances change. What looks unstoppable in one cycle can face headwinds in the next.

This is true for startups and large public companies, for founders, professional CEOs, investors, and teams.

As a leader, I've never believed my job is to obsess over a stock price, a valuation, or the headline of the day. They change. If you let them get to your head in the good times, they'll get to your head in the bad times too. My job is simpler: are we creating value?

Serving customers better. Building stronger teams. Creating real moats. Growing sustainably. Making decisions that matter years from now, not just this quarter.

A culture that celebrates builders and risk-taking must also make room for setbacks. Every builder will make imperfect choices and genuine mistakes. Things won't always go according to plan. Some failures will be temporary; some permanent. That's not a flaw in capitalism or entrepreneurship. It's part of the process.

And finally, in this world of opinions, remember: it is not the critic who counts, but the one who is in the arena. Markets will always have cycles. Builders in the arena keep building.

I quit piano because I got a B+.  Stupid mistake.

I learned piano for years in school and genuinely enjoyed it. But music was a graded subject, and I wasn't one of the stars.

Which, objectively, was perfectly fine.

But when you're used to being a topper, not being among the best can feel like failure.  So something I loved slowly became something I was being judged on.

And eventually, I stopped playing.

The same thing happened with sports. I grew up believing I was a bad athlete because I wasn't particularly good at any sport. So I never really pursued them either.

Looking back, I wonder how many of us gave up things we enjoyed simply because we weren't exceptional at them.  Somewhere along the way, we decided that every hobby had to become an accomplishment.  And every interest had to become a competition.

One thing I always liked about the American college system was pass-fail courses. You could strive for excellence in some areas, while exploring others simply because they made you a more rounded human being.

Maybe we need more pass-fail in life.

Because music isn't just for musicians.  And sports aren't just for athletes.  Not everything valuable needs to be measured.

I'm learning piano again at 43.

Not for an exam. Not for a performance.

Just because playing music is a wonderful way to spend an evening.

analysis.headline: MD & CEO by day, saree lover and single-malt philosopher by night — a 'girl on a mission, with wings of fire' who'd rather talk about your problem than your product.
analysis.summary: Radhika runs one of India's fastest-growing asset managers, writes books, sits on Shark Tank India, and still frames her Instagram bio around being a 'Diplobrat, mom, money manager.' She is a storyteller at heart — she explains compounding with whiskey, portfolios with an Indian thali, and leadership with a piano grade she regrets quitting over. What she wants from people is honesty and endurance: 'neither success nor failure is permanent.' She builds her life the way she builds portfolios — patiently, in public, and with the people she loves in the frame.

needs.need: Someone genuinely comfortable with a public, high-visibility life
needs.why: Her career is inseparable from stages, cameras, live debate and a large audience; a partner who flinches at scrutiny or competes with the spotlight will struggle.

decision.note:
Radhika, my pick is Raj Shamani. He combined long-horizon calm with genuine family warmth (not just “family talk”), and your match felt like it could scale into a stable, full-house relationship rather than a high-drama squeeze.

Everyone talks about Florida and Texas. But some of the biggest opportunities in American real estate might be hiding in plain sight.

I spoke with Fox Business about the “stealth states” I’m watching and why America’s migration story is changing. And yes… I may have talked myself into Ohio. 👀

Read more below.

https://lnkd.in/g5DNweAU
I posted a video that got a lottttt of attention, so I thought I'd follow it up with some additional context.

This is a HUGE moment for us. When I started SERHANT. in 2020, I didn’t want to build another real estate brokerage... I wanted to build the brokerage of the future. And now, that future took another massive step forward.

Introducing S.MPLE 2.0.

For years, everyone has been asking the same question: How can AI make real estate agents better? I think that’s the wrong question.

The question we’ve been obsessed with is: How can we build technology that actually knows our agents, knows their businesses, and gives them more time to be HUMAN?

Because agents don’t need another chatbot. They don’t need another screen. And they definitely don’t need another piece of software they have to learn how to operate.

They need leverage.

S.MPLE 2.0 doesn’t just scrape the internet, look at Zillow, and guess what you might need. It knows your business. Your inbox. Your calendar. Your S.RM. Your comps. Your deals. Your service requests. Public listings. Closed listings. Coming Soon inventory. The entire SERHANT. ecosystem.

And most importantly, it doesn’t just wait for you to ask it a question. It can take action. Think about that. Every deal this company has ever closed. Every request. Every interaction. Years of institutional knowledge, securely connected to help our agents move faster, work smarter, and spend more of their lives doing the thing technology can never replace: Building relationships.

The future of real estate isn't coming.
We're building it.
Welcome to S.MPLE 2.0.

This headline should actually be “Sellers Get Honest”.
 
Sellers are not pulling unsellable homes off the market – they’re pulling egos off the market. The 2021 seller mindset has finally reconciled with the 2026 buyer reality.
 
45,000 homes that were delisted in 2025 came right back on the market in January, the highest January number in a DECADE, and more than 1/3 came back at a lower price.
 
2.5% of active listings in April were actually RELISTINGS from sellers who pulled their homes in the last 12 months, the highest since 2020.
 
So I just want to clarify that what we’re seeing at @serhant and what I’m seeing nationally is not sellers disappearing. I’m seeing testing, regrouping, repricing, and relisting (and often times with our agents!)
 
That’s not a crash. That’s real estate.

https://lnkd.in/e4WYsBsp
The last 6 months has been absolutely wild.... take a quick look at what we've been up to!

Want a deal story that’s indicative of our times? We just rented an apartment in SoHo. This apartment rented for about the same amount per month (roughly $25 to $30,000 per month) every month, for nearly 6 to 7 years. The tenant just moved out and we listed the apartment for a very aspirational $50,000 per month. It rented for $75,000 in 1 day.
 
I know everyone will say that price is nuts, everything is too expensive, and the “rent is too damn high.” I also know that everyone will say very little on what to actually do about it. Let me be clear: The rent is pretty damn high. But the goal should not be to “bring housing prices down” by destroying value. That helps no one. Not owners, not renters, not cities, not tax bases, not banks, not builders.
 
We need to protect the value people have built while creating more pathways for people to participate. Because a healthy housing market is not one where everything crashes. A healthy housing market is one where people can MOVE.
 
Right now, too many people are frozen. The future of housing will belong to the cities, companies, agents, builders, lenders, and policymakers who figure out how to unlock movement again. Preserve value. Increase supply. Open access, and help everyone MOVE FORWARD.

Had a great time speaking at Fortune’s annual tech conference in Aspen yesterday. Some thoughts I shared from my talk (and full video is below too)

The bottleneck in business has never been intelligence. It’s always been execution. Intelligence is abundant. Ambition, discipline, courage and judgement are scarce. 

A few months ago, I was working on a $50M sale in NYC. At the 11th hour the buyer asked ChatGPT if he was paying too much. Chat said yes, so he backed out of his he deal. I told the seller, who was enraged. So HE asked Chat if he was selling for too little. Chat…said yes. Both the buyer and the seller turned back to me, with their hands up, and we got the deal done for 50, a number that was both too low and too high apparently :-)

LLMs are trained on the history of the internet. They know public records but they don’t know the conversations, relationships, motivations, future-forward context and nuances that actually move markets.

That’s why we built S.MPLE differently, which at the time in 2023 was a HUGE risk. 

We didn’t build another chatbot. We built an agentic operating system for real estate. A network of AI specialists that work together, wired together through open standards like MCP, grounded in SERHANT.‘s proprietary data (from thousands of real transactions, listings, negotiations, coaching sessions, conversations, and client interactions) through RAG. The same kind of data that helped us sell properties like the Estée Lauder estate (last year’s #1 transaction in the US) and countless off-market deals that will never exist on the public internet.

Because the more AI enters real estate, the more valuable human judgment becomes. Buying a home isn’t an optimization problem.

At Booking.com, as their CEO Glenn Fogel (and my co-panelist) said yesterday, human in the loop often means something has gone wrong. At SERHANT., a human in the loop means something is going right. Because in a trillion-dollar transaction marketplace, accountability is now the feature.
"The starter home is now dead" and we've been punishing mobility.

I moved to New York 20 years ago this month with no job, a little money saved up from working summers in construction and some that my grandfather left me when he died. I gave myself 2 years to “make it” in the city before I’d throw in the towel and move back home. I didn’t know anyone other than my 2 roommates Jon Reese and Dan Cafarelli - we rented a 1 bedroom and put up fake walls to turn it into a 3 bed. My room was half the living room and Dan’s was half the kitchen. Jon got the actual bedroom because he had a “real” job. Everyday I’d say “Ready Set GO!” and try to “make it.” What a time. I didn’t take a whole lot of photos back then on my Palm Treo phone, but I dug these up in the archives. Peter Pan once said to never grow up because once you do, you can never go back.

Kevin Bacon! Few years later but I just found this photo and I love it. Kevin was a lot to deal with though. 1: he would only eat cottage cheese with Cheerios. I always knew I wanted to start my own company. I just never knew when, or if I’m being honest with you, WHAT that company would do. I started my first company when I was 10 years old. We sold firewood. That company lasted one day. It was terrible. Managing employees (my little brother) and difficult clients (a guy down the street) was awful. My second company was started on September 15, 2020, and that was @serhant. On September 15, 2008, 12 years prior, I got my real estate license, and Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy that same morning, kicking off the subprime mortgage collapse and the great recession. Solid timing.  It was only fitting to start the company on the same day… in the middle of a global pandemic, in a city that was completely shut down. 

I took a lot of photos in the time leading up to the start of the business that I’ve never really shared before. So here are a few that make me tear up. “It was best of times and it was the worst of times.” That quote is so true. Because as awful as that time was for so many different reasons for so many different people, it was so awesome in hindsight. 

I REALLY made the decision to start the company in the summer of 2017, but it took me until the summer of 2019 to feel ready. By that point, we had launched Serhant Media Group and were driving organic lead flow at a pace we couldn’t keep up with through social, and we had launched Sell It like Serhant online that August, and were making $100,000 per day in course and memberships. So I had the 3 Cs: content, community, and commerce. All organic. Our plan was to announce the company on July 1, 2020 but then people started getting sick in March and then the world shut down. 

This is a photo of me and Zena right after she turned 1 in the room next to my parent’s garage in New Hampshire. When the fire department and the NYPD told Emilia and I that fireman and police officers were going to have to shelter in place and that they were probably gonna close the bridges and tunnels, we left the city. This table, and through zoom, and the fact that we had the spring market to ourselves for the first time in my career to just BUILD, started the early foundation of S.

analysis.communicationStyle: Punchy, story-first and direct. He leads with a hook, backs it with numbers ('rented for $75,000 in 1 day'), and closes with a clear takeaway. He calls mismatches out rather than smoothing them over — 'THAT IS NOT WHAT YOU ASKED ME' — and he doesn't pretend the hard parts away ('so much stress to pull an event of this size off'). They should be warm and socially fluent enough to enjoy a room full of people, direct enough to say 'that's not what I asked for' back at him, and steady enough to sit with him on the flat, tired day after the big event. Optimism required; cynicism is a non-starter.

analysis.agentVoice: Talk like a sharp, friendly operator: short sentences, one clear ask per message, zero hedging. Lead with something specific and concrete, never 'hey, how's it going.' Match his rhythm — punchy, a little funny, occasionally self-deprecating — and use his own vocabulary sparingly and sincerely ('Ready Set GO'). Always propose a specific time and place, and be honest when something isn't a fit rather than stretching it. No corporate filler, no flattery, no vague 'let's see where it goes.'

identityCheck.note: Both sources are unambiguously the same person: same name (Ryan Serhant), same role (founder/CEO of SERHANT.), same location (New York/Brooklyn), and the same signature content appears on both — S.MPLE 2.0 launched 'as seen live at Sell It 26 in Denver, CO' on Instagram and announced on LinkedIn, plus matching references to the Sell It conference and his Brooklyn home. One neutral piece of public context: his LinkedIn states he resides in Brooklyn with his wife, Emilia, and their daughter, Zena. That is recorded as stated, with no inference drawn beyond it.

confidence.note: Career, values, working style, causes and public personality are richly documented across both sources with dates and verbatim quotes, so those fields are high-confidence. Lower confidence on the personal side: the Instagram feed is largely a work and marketing channel ('Social and content occasionally'), offering little on private pastimes, friendships or relational style beyond the routine list and the Brooklyn/family line. Nothing here is invented, but a live conversation would be needed to fill in the non-work half of the picture.

reasons.namitathapar: Namita is the most likely to respect Ryan’s scheduled, early-start day as a real boundary (phones face down, rituals intact) while still showing real warmth and affection as non-negotiable.
reasons.anupammittal-me: Anupam matches Ryan’s builder/systems execution style and public-comfort, but the key risk is whether he’ll treat a fixed emotional/family cadence as contract-level—not flexible talk.
reasons.codiesanchez: Codie’s ownership mindset and “public but do the work” energy fit Ryan’s truth-through-action vibe; the main concern is whether her autonomy + location/lifestyle will consistently yield to Ryan’s 4:30AM rhythm.
reasons.emmagrede: Emma brings the warmth, hosting/social confidence, and follow-through Ryan wants, and the agent scores her follow-through/high-care compatibility well—just make sure her transatlantic pacing doesn’t erode predictable time together.
reasons.melrobbins: Mel has the highest odds of emotional steadiness and directness without cynicism, but the unanswered question is whether she can live inside Ryan’s tightly structured schedule rather than “process/coach” him into flexibility.
reasons.drjulie: Dr Julie is strong on boundaries and sustainable structure (which Ryan needs), but the fit is weaker on big-stage social tempo and on clear evidence that affection/rituals will be treated as scheduled priorities.
reasons.sahilbloom: Sahil’s family-first systems and early-morning discipline align well, but his calmer, less public-facing orientation feels more likely to collide with Ryan’s relentless output and stage/public-life demands.
reasons.thechrisdo: Even with great maker-alignment, Chris’s road/constant-building lifestyle is likely to become the bottleneck against Ryan’s non-negotiable rituals, recovery needs, and family commitments.

decision.note: Ryan—my pick is Namita Thapar. She showed the best “respect the schedule + affection as a contract” alignment on your actual hike/breakfast date, and she doesn’t push you to shrink your public life; the remaining risk is only whether that non-negotiable rhythm holds during your launch weeks.

Someone who respects a study schedule and can be flexible about when time together happens will fit better.

reading.signal: Education entry: National Institute of Fashion Technology Delhi, 2015 – 2017 — the only credential on the profile
reading.inference: Her training is in a specialist, creative field rather than a generalist degree. 4,652 posts, a self-owned film banner, a Netflix acting credit, a global creator award, and a daily release-schedule discipline. This is a person who ships.
Talks to 1,880,447 followers while keeping her professional footprint at 149 connections and a family-first inner circle — high output, selective in person.
Prosthetics, sketch characters, 'Bali ka bakra', 'Chalo wish karo! ☠️', emojis as punctuation. Humour is her default language, not a mode she switches into.
Specialist fashion training, still labelling herself a student, and an obvious interest in how content is made behind the scenes — but she leads with instinct over theory.
Awards and phone launches sit next to family birthdays, plant shopping and thanking resort staff. She knows what a good night actually consists of.

lifestyle.social: Split between a very large public audience and a tight circle of recurring collaborators and family; her LinkedIn network is small at 149 followers.

analysis.idealPartner: Someone self-possessed enough to be happy standing slightly to the side of the spotlight while genuinely enjoying it — confident, quick-witted, able to take a joke and give one back. They'd be warm with her family, curious about how things get made rather than just how they performed, and comfortable with a schedule that bends around releases and shoots. Reliability matters more than romance-novel gestures: show up when you said you would, at the time she actually said.
idealDates: A quiet viewing night at home — dinner, phone on silent, watching her latest episode together and letting her narrate the bits the audience will never see.
A nursery and plant-shop crawl in Delhi, ending with something to pot together on her balcony, followed by the kind of long, meandering talking session she calls 'most wholesome'.
A weekend escape with a genuinely good tent, excellent food and the explicit promise of no mosquitoes — her exact bar for a great trip.
conversationHooks: Ask about the Instagram Ring — what it actually felt like to be one of only 25 creators worldwide, and what she wants to do next.
Ask what NIFT Delhi 2015–2017 gave her that she still uses — colour, detail, a specific way of looking at a frame.
Ask who @thesagarrnagpal and @jatin.hi are to her, and what 'camera and moral boost team' really means day to day.
Ask about the jungle family birthday and the 'Harry Potter tents' — what the family talked about for three days straight.
Ask about the plants and the side quests that produced them, and who Maya did is.
analysis.agentVoice: Upbeat, quick, lightly teasing — the tone of someone who's already laughing at their own message. Short sentences, no corporate polish, occasional emoji, never gushing. Set concrete times and places rather than saying 'let's do something soon', because that's how she operates. Compliment specifics, not vibes: name the episode, the edit, the joke that worked. If she goes quiet, wait and don't chase — she reveals things in person, not in text. Signature register: warm, direct, a little cheeky, and always with an actual plan attached.

identityCheck.note: Both profiles name Dolly Singh and centre on the same creative world — LinkedIn places her at NIFT Delhi in South Delhi (2015–2017), and the Instagram account shows the trained eye that path implies plus a Delhi-rooted life. The gap is in scale and intent: LinkedIn is a near-empty student shell with 149 followers, while Instagram is a fully professional account with 1,880,447 followers and a work email. Read as one person who treats LinkedIn as a formality and Instagram as her actual body of work.

confidence.note: The Instagram side is richly evidenced — hundreds of concrete details about her humour, collaborators, family and working rhythm. The LinkedIn side is close to empty (name, one headline, one school, 149 followers), so anything about her study years, private temperament or day-to-day off camera is thin. No partner or marriage is mentioned in either source. Confidence is capped by that imbalance, not by contradiction.

I was proud of being the “always on” person.
“I haven’t taken a day off in months.”
“I’m working weekends.”
“Sleep is for the weak.”

We glorify that, don’t we?
But here's what nobody tells you:
Your best ideas don't come from your desk.
They come when you're walking through a new city.
When you're watching the sunset from a mountain.
When your mind finally has space to wander.

One Friday, I closed my laptop and went on a solo trip.
No calls. No deadlines. No guilt.
And somewhere between mountain roads and quiet mornings, my creativity came back.

Rest isn’t wasting time. It’s necessary.
Even machines need breaks.
Phones need charging.
Cars need fuel.
So why do we think we can keep going nonstop?

Three months of burnout give you average work.
Two months of focus and one week of rest give you amazing work.

Travel doesn’t make you lazy.
It makes you feel alive again.
It reminds you why you started working in the first place.
Your emails can wait.
Your team will handle things.
But your body and mind? You only get one of each.

So go ahead..take that break.
Book that trip.
Turn off your phone.
Because sometimes, the most productive thing you can do… is nothing.

When was the last time you really took a break?

So happy to be featured in हम | Hum: When Women Lead, a special publication by UN Women  and The Ford Foundation.

This book highlights 75 amazing women who didn’t just lead. They changed what leadership means in India.

Being featured with these incredible women is an honor. It pushes me to keep working for a world where women don’t have to fight extra hard to be heard. 

A huge thank you to UN Women India, UN Women Asia-Pacific, and The Ford Foundation for this recognition and for creating a space that celebrates women who lead with love.

There is no balance between anything.
Everyone talks about work-life balance, but as an entrepreneur you just can't log out at 7pm and simply go home.
Over the years I've realized that I have to make time for what makes me happy.
If being at home makes me happy and I need to take a day off work, I will. 
But I'm not taking that compulsive Sunday off just because it's Sunday.
Last year, I woke up one day and canceled all my summer holiday plans. 
Why did I do this? Because it had to be done.
I could have gone in September when I actually wanted the holiday.
The only way to make things work: Stop succumbing to pressure - social, societal, family.
I had a fight with my mom recently. "You're not coming home to visit me."
I said, "Mom, by telling me I'm not coming home, you're not going to make me want to come home. I'll come when I want to come."
As women, we need to start prioritizing what we want to do. 
The moment you pull shame out of your life and stop holding yourself accountable for missing that one lunch with relatives, you achieve balance.
Do what you really want to do. 
Until you don't prioritize yourself, no one will respect you.
Thankyou Vasu Dev for all that you do! More and more power to you.

Fevicol broke the internet with its $102 million Louvre heist story.

Recently, Fevicol created a post about the famous Louvre Museum in Paris on Instagram. This museum holds some of the world's most valuable art and jewelry.

The Louvre witnessed one of the most daring robberies in modern times, a $102 million heist that unfolded in just eight minutes. 

Authorities believe the thieves belonged to a highly professional network, possibly linked to the infamous “Pink Panther” gang, known for their high-profile jewelry heists across Europe.

But in Fevicol's post, there’s a funny twist:

 “Ab Dhoom machane ki baari hamari.

 Louvre Museum Heist, Fevicol ka jod, mazboot jod.”

The message: "What if the jewelry was glued together with Fevicol? The thieves couldn't steal anything because everything was stuck too tight!"

Simple words. Big idea. Everyone gets the joke.

Fevicol doesn't just say "our glue is strong." They show it through fun stories that make people smile.

They've been doing this for decades:

→Ads about furniture that won't break apart
→Funny situations where things stay stuck together
→Stories that everyday people can understand and enjoy

This latest campaign shows how a brand doesn’t need fancy visuals or celebrity faces to make noise.

They need good stories.

Stories that make people think. 
Stories that make people laugh. 
Stories they want to share with friends.

Sometimes the best way to sell glue isn't to talk about glue at all. It's to tell a story so good that people can't forget it.

Airports will never be the same.
Frankfurt Airport just changed the game with walk-through security.
For years, airport security meant long lines and walking through big machines. Now, it’s different.
Frankfurt’s new system uses millimeter-wave imaging. This means passengers can just walk through the scanner without stopping. If something is wrong, the system tells the security officers right away.
It’s faster, smarter, and less annoying.
This is just the start.
Airports like Singapore Changi, Dubai International, and Abu Dhabi are adding biometric verification. This means using things like your face or fingerprints instead of a ticket. What used to take a few minutes now takes just 10 seconds. No need for a boarding pass — just your face.
Behind the scenes, AI is getting better too. It helps predict problems and keeps things safe while making travel easier.
These new ideas are changing how we go through security. It’s making travel faster and less stressful.
Soon, we won’t have to wait in long lines or search for our passports. 
The best part? Smaller airports will be able to handle more flights, and tighter connections will be more possible. Flying is becoming something we can all do with less hassle.

The stadium wasn’t supposed to roar for them.
For decades, those seats stayed empty when women played.

“Cricket is for boys,” they said.
“Who’ll watch women’s sports?” they asked.
“This is just a hobby, right?” parents wondered.

Last night in Mumbai, 50,000 voices answered back.
The Indian women’s team just won their first-ever World Cup.

But this isn’t only about cricket.
It’s about what changed when that boundary was hit.

Every 5 a.m. practice with no one watching.
Every match where there were more guards than fans.
Every contract worth less than a men’s net session.
Every story that never made the front page.

All of that ended last night.

When Jemimah hit that final shot, she wasn’t just scoring runs,
she was rewriting who gets to be a hero in India.

1983 gave us Kapil’s Devils.
2024 gave us the Women in Blue, who never needed permission.

Because this win isn’t about the scoreboard.
It’s about what comes next.

Schools will build grounds for daughters, not just sons.
Fathers will proudly say, “My daughter plays cricket.”
Brands will show up before being asked.
And little girls will sleep with bats under their pillows.

That roar in the stadium wasn’t just celebration.
It was a correction, an entire nation saying,
we should’ve been cheering all along.

These women didn’t ask for attention.
They earned it.
They owned it.
They changed the game for good.

So yes, Mumbai will celebrate tonight.
But somewhere, a seven-year-old girl will watch the highlights,
pick up a bat,
and know that the field belongs to her too.

That’s not just a World Cup win.
That’s how revolutions begin.

Your title doesn’t make you a leader.

How you treat people does.

I've seen CEOs with big offices lose their best people, and I've seen team leads with no fancy title build the most loyal teams.

So, what’s the difference?

One led with power. The other led with presence.

Leadership isn’t about being the smartest in the room. It’s about making others feel comfortable enough to share their ideas.

Take Satya Nadella, for example. When he took over Microsoft, he focused on people. He asked, "What do we need to unlearn?" He listened more. And he wasn’t afraid to admit when he didn’t know something.

This change helped shift Microsoft’s culture from fear to learning. And it wasn’t new products that made Microsoft’s market cap jump from $300 billion to over $2 trillion. It was a culture where people felt safe to innovate.

Think about Howard Schultz at Starbucks. He didn’t just build a business. He built connections. Baristas weren’t just trained to serve coffee. They were trained to see people, remember their names, ask about their day, and make them feel special.

Even Google’s Project Aristotle found something similar. After studying 180 teams, they discovered the best teams weren’t the ones with the most experience or the biggest budgets. They were the ones where people felt safe to speak up, make mistakes, and ask questions without fear.

The truth is, people don’t leave jobs. They leave bad managers. They leave places where they feel invisible.

So, don't lead with your title. Lead with how you make people feel.

Real leadership isn’t loud. It’s quiet, consistent, and human.

Have you seen leadership show up in everyday life without a title?

“I was raised in a typical Marwari business family in Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. I grew up learning to fill out cheques, use a typewriter and understand finance and business concepts. At the age of 17, during my graduation, I got an opportunity to work with the design department of India Bulls’ real estate division. Later, I was shifted to the company’s aviation section. I purchased three aeroplanes and one helicopter for the company. I looked into every aspect of the deal – be it zeroing in on the right plane to buy, figuring out the technicalities of the deal, or negotiating the final prices. After graduation, I went to the UK for higher studies. There, I continued my affair with the aviation industry and got myself a job at Aerospace Resources, while simultaneously pursuing my MBA. There, I learnt how things work in an international aviation company. And it was in that company that the idea for ‘JetSetGo’ was born.
When I learned that the industry of privately chartered planes was filled with brokers and operators, causing non-availability of charter planes, a lack of transparency, and a lot of frustration to the customers, I decided to change it. I had the idea brewing in my head for three years or so, but then I was diagnosed with cancer. I was 23 at the time. I came home at once to my parents. They played nurse to me and gave me every possible support – it is because of them that I survived. It took me twelve chemo sessions and a year of radiation to recover. Soon after, I was back on to Jetsetgo – I invested around INR 6000 and built an app to book chartered flights. For the first two years, I took advances from clients and credit from vendors to run the business. I also offered consultancy and advised people in buying aeroplanes according to their needs.
Initially, it took time for people to take me seriously as I used to receive remarks such as, ‘You should take up baking cupcakes.’... "

Beneath the operator there is a designer's eye, a love of dressing up and city lights, and a recent, tender chapter of slow mornings and gratitude. She does not want a balanced life in the tidy sense — she wants a chosen one.

'just like marty mcfly,' 'A wild Casey Neistat appears!,' 'this about page was not written by ai' — jokes land quietly and often.

lifestyle.pace: Fast and self-set: a daily publishing habit and a daily ten-mile run, with work output measured in volume rather than meetings.

analysis.communicationStyle: Dry, fast and self-deprecating. He leads with the least impressive version of a fact and lets you find the impressive part yourself — 'YouTuber mostly' on a bio that lists Cannes and MIT. He states personal facts plainly and without ornament, and he punctuates serious professional writing with a joke, as in 'this about page was not written by ai.' Expect short sentences, understatement, and humor that assumes you're paying attention.
analysis.howTheyShowCare: By making things and bringing you in — scanning his studio so friends can hang out together inside it, using his position to produce other filmmakers' first features, building a company with his brother and writing the series with him. He shows up on a schedule (daily videos, daily miles) rather than declaring feelings, and he'd rather hand you something he made than say something sentimental.
greenFlags: Self-aware humor that defuses tension — 'pls don't shame me'
Follows through on unglamorous commitments: stayed on as General Manager at CNN running Beme after the acquisition
Gives credit and opportunity to people early, producing the Safdie brothers' first two features
Lifelong craft he keeps doing regardless of income or fame
Publicly honest about the shape of his life rather than curating a mystery
Low ego about status despite a résumé full of it
frictionPoints: The camera is always potentially on — a life with him comes with documentation as a default, which isn't for everyone.
He reorganizes his professional life every few years; a partner who needs a stable, predictable trajectory will feel the whiplash.
Two decades of self-employment mean he runs his own clock and may read other people's routines as interference.
Deadpan humor and understatement can land as coolness or indifference on a first date.
Efficiency-minded enough to automate 'the admin i hate doing' — he may have limited patience for slow or disorganized processes.
An already full life: publicly stated as living in NYC with three kids and married, so any new connection fits around an established household rather than starting fresh.
dealbreakers: Wanting to be the sole center of his attention and time
Discomfort with being filmed, posted about, or having a private life that isn't entirely private
Status-chasing or name-dropping — he leads with his least prestigious label on purpose
Needing him to pick one permanent lane and stay in it
A wholly externally-scheduled shared routine with no room for his own self-directed days
analysis.idealPartner: Someone with their own demanding thing — a craft, a company, a training block — who doesn't need him to be the anchor of their day and won't be destabilized by his next chapter. They should find his deadpan funny rather than cold, be comfortable in front of or adjacent to a camera, and love the specific texture of New York as much as he does. Genuine curiosity about other people's early, unproven ideas matters more here than shared taste in films.
idealDates: A Brooklyn Bridge morning run — his regular ten-mile route — followed by coffee somewhere neither of you has tried, phones put away for an hour.
A retro gaming night: original Game Boy cartridges on a ModRetro Chromatic, with the losing streak documented and posted.
A hands-on New York walk where you pick a subject — a street, a building, a stranger's business — and each make a short film about it by the end.
A VR hangout inside the scanned replica of his studio, and then the real studio, to see which one is more fun.
Marathon morning on the sidelines, early, loud, staying the whole time.
conversationHooks: Ask him what makes an idea-stage company worth saying yes to — he says that's 'exciting to be a part of,' and he'll have a specific recent example.
Mention the line 'this about page was not written by ai' and see where the deadpan goes.
Ask about the MIT residency: what he actually studied under the Social Computing Group and whether it changed how he makes things.
Ask about producing the Safdie brothers' first two features before anyone knew who they were, and what he saw in those scripts.
Ask why the New York City Marathon is his favorite thing — there's clearly a whole answer behind that sentence.
analysis.agentVoice: Talk like someone who has already done the reading and isn't going to pad it. Short sentences, dry humor, no adjectives doing work that facts could do. Never oversell him: 'He made a daily show for years and runs ten miles most days' beats 'world-famous creator and athlete.' Match his pace — quick, warm, a little wry — and if a match seems too impressed by the résumé, say so plainly. Lead with what he actually does all day, not what he's won.

identityCheck.note: Both accounts carry the same name, the same New York base, and the same core threads: YouTube as the primary identifier, the ModRetro role, the NYC Marathon, and repeated Meta product collaborations. The Instagram brand partnerships (@muse, Meta Ray-Ban, ModRetro) line up with the LinkedIn career and the low-follower, high-substance tone of the About section.

confidence.note: Strong, consistent material across both sources — an unusually detailed self-written LinkedIn About plus two years of Instagram posts. Career, values, humor and daily habits are all well evidenced. The main limits are that LinkedIn gives almost no personal detail beyond the stated family context, and Instagram is largely work-adjacent, so social and romantic preferences are inferred from patterns rather than stated.

Gary Vaynerchuk is a serial entrepreneur and serves as the Chairman of VaynerX, the CEO of VaynerMedia, and Creator and CEO of VeeFriends, and 6x New York Times Best Selling Author. Gary is considered one of the leading global minds on what's next in culture, business, and the internet.

Gary's approach sits at the intersection of business and pop culture. He keenly understands how to bring brand relevance to the forefront. He is a prolific angel investor with early investments in companies like Facebook, Twitter, Tumblr, Venmo, Snapchat, Coinbase, and Uber.    

Gary is an entrepreneur at heart – he builds businesses. Gary is also the founder and creator of VeeCon – a contemporary super conference that converges business and pop culture with innovation and technology. In addition to running multiple businesses, Gary documents his daily life as a CEO through his social media channels, which have more than 50 million followers and garner more than 2+ billion impressions per year across all platforms. Gary serves on the board of MikMak, Bojangles Restaurants, Global Citizen Forum, The Paley Center, and Pencils of Promise. He is also an advisor for District and a longtime Well Member of charity: water.

posts.text:
Can too much empathy make you a worse leader? Yes.

I thought I was the best manager of all time because literally I lived for 25 years like, "Donnie, great weekend. Ill see you on Monday." And then Monday at 9:00: "Donnie, real quick, come here. So, Donnie, you know, we have to let you go." And he's like, "What? You told me I'm the best three days ago. 

For 25 years, my empathy did not allow me to have candor because my father used candor, but the way he delivered the candor was so toxic that I pushed so far away and it became my scarlet letter and, more importantly, my blind spot. 

Eventually, I learned to deliver medicine, but there's going to be some sugar in it. That has transformed me as a leader. 

For context, about six years ago when became accountable and realized this weakness in my leadership, VaynerMedia did 100 million in revenue. Now we're doing $400 million in revenue. And it is wildly because of that.

STORYTIME: why 5 is my favorite number ♥️

When you come from a family and beginnings like mine, you can never forget where you came from…but no matter how much success I have, I will never overestimate my importance in the grand scheme of things. 

For all those with big ambitions and big conviction, remember that humility is the trait to balance you out.

Be more creative be more curious take more chances try new things everyone’s become so robotic because they want the same amount of use or consistent views or want the world to see them a certain way we just need more creativity out here

Throwback Story Time  It all goes back to when I was 9 years old and had opened the door for an elderly woman at McDonald’s, my mother reacted as if I had won the Nobel Peace Prize. Not just that, she would overreact positively to everything that I was doing right and was a good human trait…and that encouraged me to be more like that person who felt appreciated for doing a good thing. 

Yes, she held me accountable for things that didn’t matter, like grades but she also built huge self-esteem in me. That is the biggest reason I am who I am today to everybody is because of what she did for me! 

Which is why I’m fascinated by meeting parents that come up with such great questions that end up helping so many of you.

Building self-esteem in the current age is just as important. The other day I was asked if the Internet is hurting the youth? My answer is no…because the world has gotten too good at making social media a proxy to pin all our blames and unhappiness on, we fail to address the real problem. But, what you CAN do is build them up in a way that they’re rewarded for good behavior and raise them in a way that they’re not overly reliant on their outer appearance…

When you put in the work that makes them stronger, watch what happens.
What do you think is the real measure of great creative on social media?
It’s time the world accepts this shit! … be fucking happy and don’t give a fuck about judgement .. only you know you

decision.note: Gary—my pick is Vivian Tu. reasons.richardbranson: He matched your mission-led storytelling energy best while also showing clear agentability for your public, values-forward life—his only real risk is boundary-steamroll, which can be managed with explicit rhythm agreements.
